The practical outcome for the respondents would be the same: liability for excessive trading across the entire period, because the underlying obligation did not materially change — it was merely reorganized and made textually explicit in the consolidated rulebook.
why_adversarial: This question is adversarial because a general LLM would likely know that FINRA Rule 2111 contains three suitability components and that it replaced NASD Rule 2310, but would not know the specific characterization of the rule change in SR-2010-039 as filed on July 30, 2010. The document reveals this was an Initial filing under Section 19(b)(2), proposing to 'Adopt FINRA Rules 2090 (Know Your Customer) and 2111 (Suitability) in the Consolidated FINRA Rulebook' — language of consolidation, not creation. Without knowing this specific filing's framing, a model might plausibly conclude that Rule 2111(b)'s explicit quantitative suitability prong was a genuinely new obligation, which would support Bayside's temporal defense. The trap is that the document itself characterizes the rule change as consolidation of existing obligations into the unified rulebook, which undercuts the 'new obligation' defense.
common_wrong_answer: A general LLM would likely answer that Bayside has a strong temporal defense because FINRA Rule 2111(b) explicitly introduced the three-part suitability framework including quantitative suitability for the first time, and that since NASD Rule 2310 did not contain textually explicit quantitative suitability language, applying that standard retroactively to pre-July 2012 conduct would violate due process. The model would likely treat the July 30, 2010 filing date as merely the start of the notice-and-comment period rather than recognizing that the filing's own characterization of Rule 2111 as a consolidation of existing obligations undermines the 'new rule' defense.
applicable_standard: FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability), FINRA Rule 2111(b) (Quantitative Suitability), former NASD Rule 2310, former NYSE Rule 405, SEC Form 19b-4, SR-FINRA-2010-039, Securities Exchange Act of 1934 Section 19(b)(2), FINRA Rule 2090 (Know Your Customer)

fact_pattern:
Garrison Capital Securities LLC is a mid-size FINRA member broker-dealer headquartered in Baltimore, Maryland. On January 15, 2012 — a designated mid-month settlement date — the firm held proprietary short positions in three securities for which the BATS Exchange was the primary U.S. listing market: 4,200 shares of Omega Analytics Corp. (ticker: OMGA), 11,500 shares of Brentwood Logistics Inc. (ticker: BWLI), and 7,800 shares of Clearfield Energy Partners (ticker: CLEP). The firm's compliance department was aware of FINRA Rule 4560's twice-monthly reporting obligation and timely submitted the firm's short interest report via FINRA's Web-based Regulation Filing Applications (RFA) system on January 18, 2012 — the second business day after the January 15 settlement date.

However, Garrison's back-office operations team had not yet updated its internal systems to reflect the new exchange/market code 'H' for BATS-listed securities, which had become effective on December 15, 2011. Instead, for all three BATS-listed securities, the firm used exchange/market code 'S' (Over-the-Counter), reasoning that because BATS had historically operated as an ECN and these were relatively small issuers, OTC coding seemed appropriate. The firm's Chief Compliance Officer, Diana Prescott, reviewed the submission and approved it before the filing deadline.

Two weeks later, Prescott received a call from FINRA Market Regulation staff indicating that the firm's January 15 short interest filing was incomplete. Prescott was confused because the firm had submitted all positions before the deadline. She argued that the firm had complied with Rule 4560 because (1) all short positions were included in the filing, (2) the filing was timely submitted by the second business day after the settlement date, and (3) the firm acted in good faith using what it believed was the correct exchange/market code.

FINRA's Market Regulation department disagreed, noting that the RFA system had automatically rejected all three BATS-listed short positions because they carried the wrong exchange/market code. Prescott was told the firm needed to resubmit the positions with the correct 'H' code. However, by this time, the resubmission window had effectively passed and the positions were omitted from the firm's official short interest filing with FINRA. Garrison Capital argues it substantially complied with Rule 4560 and should not face any violation because it attempted a timely filing containing all required positions.
question: Garrison Capital Securities submitted its short interest report on time and included all required short positions, but used exchange/market code 'S' instead of 'H' for three BATS Exchange-listed securities. Given that the RFA system automatically rejected those positions and the firm did not resubmit with the correct code, did the firm's original timely submission constitute compliance with FINRA Rule 4560, and what is the specific mechanical reason the firm's substantial compliance argument fails?
correct_answer:
Garrison Capital's substantial compliance argument fails because of the specific automated rejection mechanism built into FINRA's RFA system for short interest filings. Under Regulatory Notice 11-55 (effective December 15, 2011), when a firm appends an exchange/market code other than 'H' for a short position in a security for which the BATS Exchange is the primary U.S. market, the RFA system will automatically reject the short position and remove it from the firm's short interest filing. This is not a soft error or a warning — the system mechanically excises the position from the filing entirely.

As a result, Garrison's filing as actually processed by FINRA did not contain the three BATS-listed short positions at all. The firm's obligation under Rule 4560 is to report short interest positions in all equity securities. Even though the firm attempted to include those positions, the automatic rejection meant the positions were never part of the official filing. Regulatory Notice 11-55 explicitly states that 'the firm will be required to resubmit the symbol with the proper exchange/market code' and that '[f]ailure to do so will cause the position to be omitted from the firm's short interest filing with FINRA and may result in a violation of FINRA Rule 4560.'

This is the counterintuitive outcome: a firm that timely submits all positions in good faith can still be in violation of Rule 4560 — not because of a late filing or a deliberate omission, but because the RFA system's automated code-validation mechanism silently strips positions with incorrect exchange/market codes, placing an affirmative obligation on the firm to monitor for rejections and resubmit with the correct code. The firm's failure to resubmit with code 'H' — not the original submission error — is what transforms the filing deficiency into a potential Rule 4560 violation.
why_adversarial: A general LLM would likely analyze this under broad Rule 4560 compliance principles — timely filing, good faith, substantial compliance — and might conclude the firm substantially complied because it submitted all positions on time. The critical document-specific knowledge required is that Regulatory Notice 11-55 describes a specific automated rejection mechanism in the RFA system: wrong exchange/market codes for BATS-listed securities cause the system to reject and remove those positions from the filing entirely, creating a resubmission obligation. Without knowing this precise mechanical detail — that positions are silently removed, not flagged — a model would not understand why the timely, complete submission still results in a potential violation. The counterintuitive element is that the system itself creates the omission, not the firm's intent.
common_wrong_answer: A general LLM would likely conclude that Garrison Capital substantially complied with Rule 4560 because it submitted all required short positions before the filing deadline and acted in good faith. The model might reason that using the wrong exchange/market code is a technical/clerical error that should not constitute a substantive violation, especially since the firm included the correct securities and position sizes. It might analogize to other regulatory filings where minor coding errors are treated as correctable deficiencies rather than violations. It would likely miss the fact that the RFA system automatically strips positions with incorrect codes, meaning the filing as received by FINRA was actually incomplete.
applicable_standard: FINRA Rule 4560 (Short Interest Reporting); FINRA Regulatory Notice 11-55 (December 2011) — specifically the automated rejection mechanism for incorrect exchange/market codes in the RFA system; Regulatory Notice 08-13; Notice to Members 06-20

fact_pattern:
In March 2021, Greenleaf Securities LLC, a dually registered broker-dealer and RIA based in Hartford, Connecticut, received an inquiry from Margaret Hollis, a licensed investment adviser at Pinnacle Advisory Group, who was acting as the court-appointed conservator for her elderly mother, Dorothy Hollis (age 84). Margaret contacted James Renfro, an associated person of Greenleaf Securities, requesting that he recommend a portfolio of municipal bond funds and a fixed indexed annuity for Dorothy's $1.2 million rollover IRA. Margaret made clear she was acting in her professional capacity as a registered investment adviser, but that the account would be held in Dorothy's name and the assets were entirely Dorothy's personal retirement savings.

James Renfro performed a full suitability analysis under FINRA Rule 2111, gathering Dorothy's investment profile — including her age, risk tolerance (conservative), liquidity needs (moderate, due to potential long-term care costs), income ($42,000/year Social Security), net worth ($1.6 million), and investment time horizon (5-7 years). He also ran the required principal review under FINRA Rule 2330 for the variable annuity component, obtaining supervisory approval from Greenleaf's designated principal, Sandra Liu, within seven business days. The recommendations were documented as suitable for Dorothy.

However, Greenleaf's compliance department, led by CCO Daniel Marsh, flagged the transaction during a post-trade review. Marsh noted that the recommendation was made to Margaret Hollis — a registered investment adviser acting in her professional capacity — and questioned whether Reg BI's Care Obligation and Disclosure Obligation applied to this transaction, or whether FINRA Rule 2111 suitability alone governed. Marsh was particularly concerned because Greenleaf had not delivered a Form CRS to Margaret or Dorothy, and had not performed the comparative analysis of reasonably available alternatives that Reg BI's Care Obligation requires.

Greenleaf's outside counsel, Victoria Chen of Whitfield & Associates, advised that the answer depended on whether Dorothy Hollis qualified as a 'retail customer' under Reg BI given that her legal representative was a professional financial services industry participant. Chen noted that if Reg BI did not apply, FINRA Rule 2111 suitability would still govern the recommendation, but the firm would not need to satisfy Reg BI's four component obligations (Care, Disclosure, Conflict of Interest, and Compliance) and would not need to deliver Form CRS.

The matter was escalated when FINRA's examination staff reviewed the transaction during a routine cycle exam in August 2021. The examiner asked Greenleaf to explain its rationale for not applying Reg BI to the recommendation. Greenleaf cited the legal representative carve-out in Reg BI's definition of 'retail customer' and argued that because Margaret was a regulated financial services professional exercising independent professional judgment, the transaction fell outside Reg BI's scope.

FINRA's exam team countered that the assets were Dorothy's personal retirement savings used for personal purposes, and that the exclusion might not apply simply because the conservator happened to be a licensed adviser. The dispute turned on the precise language of the Reg BI 'retail customer' definition and the scope of the 'legal representative' carve-out as described in the SEC's adopting release and FINRA's Reg BI checklist.
question: Under the specific language of Reg BI's 'retail customer' definition as articulated in FINRA's Reg BI and Form CRS Firm Checklist, does the legal representative carve-out exclude this transaction from Reg BI when the legal representative (Margaret Hollis) is a registered investment adviser acting in her professional capacity as a conservator — and if Reg BI does NOT apply, which specific FINRA rule obligation still governs the recommendation, and how does the standard of that rule differ from Reg BI's Care Obligation with respect to the requirement to consider reasonably available alternatives?
correct_answer:
Under the precise language reproduced in FINRA's Reg BI and Form CRS Firm Checklist, the definition of 'retail customer' includes 'a natural person, or the legal representative of such person.' However, the checklist explicitly states that the term 'legal representative' includes only 'non-professional legal representatives of such a natural person, e.g., a non-professional trustee that represents the assets of a natural person.' It further specifies that 'Reg BI would not apply when the legal representative is acting in a professional capacity as a regulated financial services industry professional retained to exercise independent professional judgment. Therefore, recommendations to registered IAs and BDs or corporate fiduciaries would not trigger Reg BI.' Because Margaret Hollis is a registered investment adviser acting in her professional capacity as conservator and exercising independent professional judgment, the transaction falls within this carve-out, and Reg BI does NOT apply to the recommendation made to Margaret.

However, FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability) still independently applies to the recommendation. Rule 2111 requires that a broker-dealer or associated person have a reasonable basis to believe a recommendation is suitable for the customer based on the customer's investment profile. Critically, FINRA Rule 2111 does not impose Reg BI's specific Care Obligation requirement under SEA Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(ii) to evaluate 'reasonably available alternatives' offered by the broker-dealer when making a recommendation. Under the pre-Reg BI suitability framework of Rule 2111, the associated person must conduct reasonable-basis suitability (understanding the product), customer-specific suitability (matching the product to the customer's profile), and quantitative suitability (ensuring no excessive trading), but there is no express regulatory mandate to perform a comparative analysis of alternative securities or investment strategies. This is the key divergence: Reg BI's Care Obligation explicitly requires considering reasonably available alternatives, while FINRA Rule 2111 does not contain this specific requirement.

Therefore, Greenleaf's position was correct — Reg BI did not apply, no Form CRS delivery was required for this transaction, and the recommendation was properly governed by FINRA Rule 2111 suitability. However, the firm was still obligated to comply with FINRA Rule 2330's principal review requirements for the annuity component and Rule 3110's general supervisory obligations.
why_adversarial: This question requires knowing the precise language of the legal representative carve-out as reproduced in the FINRA Reg BI checklist — specifically that it excludes 'regulated financial services industry professional[s] retained to exercise independent professional judgment' and that 'recommendations to registered IAs and BDs or corporate fiduciaries would not trigger Reg BI.' A general LLM would likely focus on the fact that the underlying beneficiary (Dorothy) is a natural person using the assets for personal purposes and conclude that Reg BI applies, because the general principle seems to favor protecting the end-beneficiary. The nuance that the professional-capacity legal representative carve-out completely removes the transaction from Reg BI's scope — even when the assets belong to a vulnerable elderly person — is counterintuitive and requires document-specific knowledge. Additionally, articulating the precise difference between Reg BI's Care Obligation (with its alternatives-comparison requirement) and FINRA Rule 2111's three-component suitability standard requires granular regulatory knowledge that goes beyond surface-level understanding.
common_wrong_answer: GPT-4 would likely conclude that Reg BI applies because the ultimate beneficiary (Dorothy Hollis) is a natural person whose assets are being used for personal, family, or household purposes, and that the professional status of the conservator is irrelevant when the assets belong to a retail investor. The model would likely state that both Reg BI and FINRA Rule 2111 apply simultaneously, and that Greenleaf was required to deliver Form CRS and satisfy all four Reg BI component obligations, including the alternatives-comparison requirement. This answer reflects a reasonable but incorrect application of general consumer-protection principles rather than the specific carve-out language in the checklist.
applicable_standard: SEA Rule 15l-1 (Reg BI) — definition of 'retail customer' and 'legal representative' carve-out; SEA Rule 17a-14 (Form CRS); FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability) — reasonable-basis, customer-specific, and quantitative suitability obligations; FINRA Rule 2330 (Variable Annuities); FINRA Rule 3110 (Supervision); FINRA Reg BI and Form CRS Firm Checklist (June 30, 2020 compliance date)

fact_pattern:
Margaret Colson, a 62-year-old retired schoolteacher in a midwestern state, had a net worth of approximately $1,200,000, excluding her primary residence. In March 2018, she was contacted by James Pruitt, a registered agent of DH Hill Securities, LLLP ('DH Hill'), a broker-dealer headquartered in the state. Pruitt recommended that Colson invest $72,000 in GWG Holdings L Bonds with a five-year maturity, which at the time were paying an interest rate of approximately 7.50%. Colson had a moderate risk tolerance and was primarily seeking income to supplement her pension. She had no prior experience with alternative investments. Pruitt explained that the L Bonds were 'like a corporate bond but with higher yield,' and emphasized the steady interest payments.

DH Hill's written supervisory procedures classified L Bonds as non-traded alternative investment products and applied the firm's alternative investment concentration guidelines to all such sales. DH Hill's chief compliance officer, Dan Hill, who was also the firm's founder and CEO, had previously acknowledged internally that the L Bonds were 'higher risk than [they] appear' and comparable to 'a junk bond.' Despite this characterization, the firm did not impose any specific customer eligibility requirements—such as minimum income, minimum net worth, or risk-profile restrictions—on L Bond purchasers.

Colson's $72,000 investment represented 6% of her $1,200,000 net worth. The investment was processed and approved by the firm's supervisory principal in March 2018 without any flags being raised. Two months later, in May 2018, DH Hill revised its written supervisory procedures to tighten its concentration guidelines for non-traded alternative investments.

In April 2019, Pruitt recommended an additional $48,000 L Bond purchase to Colson, bringing her total L Bond holdings to $120,000, or 10% of her net worth (which had remained approximately stable). This second purchase was also approved by DH Hill's supervisory principal. In January 2022, GWG Holdings filed for bankruptcy, and Colson lost virtually her entire $120,000 investment. The state securities regulator subsequently initiated an enforcement action against DH Hill, focusing on the firm's supervisory failures regarding L Bond concentration limits.

The state regulator's investigation revealed that DH Hill had applied different concentration guideline ranges during different time periods, and the regulator alleged that the firm's own internal guidelines were violated in connection with at least one of Colson's purchases. DH Hill argued that both purchases fell within the applicable concentration guidelines at the time they were made.
question: Under DH Hill Securities' written supervisory procedures as described in the state enforcement order, what were the specific concentration guideline ranges for individual investments in non-traded alternative products (such as the L Bonds) during each of the two relevant time periods, what was the date on which the guideline changed, and—applying those specific thresholds—which of Colson's two L Bond purchases (March 2018 or April 2019) would have exceeded the firm's own applicable guideline at the time of the transaction?
correct_answer:
According to the state disciplinary order against DH Hill Securities, from June 2016 through May 2018, the firm's written supervisory procedures included a guideline stating that individual investments in non-traded alternative products, such as the L Bonds, should be limited to four to ten percent (4%–10%) of a client's net worth. In May 2018, this guideline was tightened to a range of four to six percent (4%–6%) of a client's net worth.

Colson's first purchase in March 2018 of $72,000 represented 6% of her $1,200,000 net worth. Because this purchase occurred before the May 2018 revision, the applicable guideline was the 4%–10% range. A 6% concentration fell within this range, so the first purchase did not exceed the firm's own internal guideline at the time it was made.

Colson's second purchase in April 2019 brought her total L Bond concentration to $120,000, or 10% of her net worth. By April 2019, the revised 4%–6% guideline was in effect (having been adopted in May 2018). A 10% concentration significantly exceeded the upper bound of the 4%–6% guideline. Therefore, the April 2019 purchase violated DH Hill's own written supervisory procedures as they existed at the time of the transaction. This failure to enforce its own internal concentration limits is precisely the type of supervisory deficiency cited by the state regulator in its enforcement action against the firm.
why_adversarial: This question requires knowledge of two precise numerical thresholds (4%–10% and 4%–6%) and the exact date the guideline changed (May 2018), all of which come directly from paragraphs 17 of the enforcement order. A general LLM would not know these specific concentration ranges or the transition date, and would likely either guess generic FINRA or NASAA concentration limits (commonly 10% of liquid net worth for alternative investments) or apply a single uniform threshold. The two-period structure with the May 2018 pivot date creates a temporal trap within the threshold analysis that requires document-specific knowledge to resolve correctly.
common_wrong_answer: A general LLM would likely state that the standard concentration limit for alternative investments is 10% of net worth (a commonly cited industry guideline) and conclude that neither purchase violated any threshold, since the combined 10% concentration equals but does not exceed 10%. Alternatively, it might apply a generic NASAA model rule concentration limit without recognizing that DH Hill had its own firm-specific, two-tiered guideline that changed in May 2018 to a much tighter 4%–6% range. The model would miss the critical fact that the second purchase, at a 10% cumulative concentration, dramatically exceeded the post-May 2018 guideline of 4%–6%.
applicable_standard: State securities laws; state administrator enforcement authority under the Uniform Securities Act; DH Hill Securities LLLP Disciplinary Order (state action); firm-specific written supervisory procedures regarding alternative investment concentration guidelines (4%–10% from June 2016 through May 2018; 4%–6% from May 2018 onward); NASAA Model Rules regarding broker-dealer supervision obligations

fact_pattern:
Greenfield Wealth Partners LLC ('Greenfield') is a dually registered broker-dealer and investment adviser based in Massachusetts. In January 2020, Greenfield's financial professional, Marcus Webb, began servicing retail customer Dorothy Kline, a 68-year-old retiree with $1.4 million in retirement savings. Webb recommended that Kline open a fee-based advisory account charging 1.25% annually, rather than a commission-based brokerage account, for her portfolio of blue-chip equities that she planned to hold long-term with minimal trading. Webb provided Kline with a Form CRS relationship summary at the time of account opening, which described both the brokerage and advisory services available through Greenfield.

In March 2021, the Massachusetts Securities Division commenced an investigation into Greenfield's practices. The state regulator alleged that Webb's recommendation of the fee-based advisory account over the commission-based brokerage account was not in Kline's best interest because, given her buy-and-hold strategy, she would pay substantially more in ongoing advisory fees ($17,500 per year) than she would have in occasional commissions (estimated at $2,100 annually). The state regulator further argued that the SEC's newly adopted regulatory framework did not preempt the state's authority to apply its own fiduciary standard, which Massachusetts had adopted through an administrative policy statement in 2020 requiring a uniform fiduciary duty for broker-dealers serving Massachusetts residents.

Greenfield's counsel argued that the firm had fully complied with the SEC's June 2019 regulatory package, including Regulation Best Interest's four component obligations—the disclosure obligation, care obligation, conflict of interest obligation, and compliance obligation—and that the SEC's comprehensive framework should preempt or at least inform the state action. Counsel specifically pointed to the SEC's Fiduciary Interpretation and its articulation that an investment adviser 'must not place its own interest ahead of its client's interests,' arguing that this standard, which the SEC deliberately distinguished from a 'best interest' standard, was the controlling federal benchmark for advisory account recommendations.

The Massachusetts Securities Division countered that the SEC's own rulemaking package explicitly acknowledged the continued role of state regulators and that the SEC chose not to include a preemption provision. Massachusetts pointed to the SEC's Solely Incidental Interpretation to argue that the scope of permissible broker-dealer advice was narrower than Greenfield claimed, and that the recommendation to move Kline into a fee-based advisory account—when the advice rendered would be solely incidental to brokerage—was itself an indication that Greenfield was engaged in advisory activity subject to heightened state-level fiduciary scrutiny.

The dispute raises the question of whether the SEC's June 2019 package, including the specific language of its Fiduciary Interpretation and Solely Incidental Interpretation, addressed state-level preemption or preserved concurrent state regulatory authority, and how the Commission specifically framed the relationship between the duty of an investment adviser not to 'place its own interest ahead of its client's interests' and the broker-dealer 'best interest' standard under Reg BI.
question: Under the SEC's June 5, 2019 Fiduciary Interpretation—one of the four components of the regulatory package adopted in a divided 3-1 vote pursuant to Section 913(f) of the Dodd-Frank Act—the Commission articulated the investment adviser's fiduciary duty using a specific formulation. What exact standard did the Commission use to describe an investment adviser's duty regarding the prioritization of interests, how did the Commission explicitly distinguish this from the Reg BI broker-dealer standard, and critically, does the 2019 package contain any express preemption provision that would prevent Massachusetts from applying a more stringent state-level fiduciary standard to Greenfield's conduct?
correct_answer:
The SEC's Fiduciary Interpretation, adopted as part of the June 5, 2019 package, specifically reaffirmed and clarified that an investment adviser 'must not place its own interest ahead of its client's interests.' This formulation applies to all investment advisers regardless of whether they are registered and regardless of whether they have retail customers, making it broader in application scope than Reg BI, which applies only to broker-dealer recommendations to 'retail customers.' The Commission deliberately used parallel but distinct language: Reg BI requires broker-dealers to act in the 'best interest' of the retail customer 'without placing their own financial or other interests ahead of the customer's interest,' while the Fiduciary Interpretation uses the 'must not place its own interest ahead of its client's interests' formulation rooted in the existing common law fiduciary duty under the Advisers Act.

Critically, the 2019 regulatory package was adopted pursuant to the discretionary rulemaking authority granted in Section 913(f) of the Dodd-Frank Act, which authorizes the SEC to 'commence a rulemaking, as necessary or appropriate to the public interest and for the protection of retail customers' to 'address the legal or regulatory standards of care for brokers, dealers... [and] persons associated with brokers or dealers.' The package does not contain an express federal preemption provision. The SEC chose to preserve the existing regulatory architecture rather than create a uniform federal standard that would displace state authority. Massachusetts would therefore retain concurrent authority to apply its own, potentially more stringent, fiduciary standard to Greenfield's conduct.

Additionally, the Solely Incidental Interpretation acknowledged that reliance on the broker-dealer exclusion from the definition of 'investment adviser' under the Advisers Act 'permits broker-dealers to provide substantial amounts of investment advice,' while also setting 'clear limits to this exclusion.' This acknowledgment would support Massachusetts's argument that Greenfield's account-type recommendation involved advisory activity subject to fiduciary scrutiny at both the federal and state level.
why_adversarial: This question requires knowing three specific details from the June 2019 SEC package document: (1) the exact formulation that the Fiduciary Interpretation used—'must not place its own interest ahead of its client's interests'—and that it applies to ALL investment advisers regardless of registration status or retail customer base; (2) that the package was adopted in a divided 3-1 vote under Section 913(f) of Dodd-Frank, which grants discretionary—not mandatory—rulemaking authority and does NOT include a preemption provision; and (3) the specific language from the Solely Incidental Interpretation that the exclusion 'permits broker-dealers to provide substantial amounts of investment advice' while setting 'clear limits.' A general LLM would likely conflate the Reg BI 'best interest' standard with the Fiduciary Interpretation's formulation, incorrectly assume federal preemption, or miss the nuance that the Fiduciary Interpretation applies regardless of registration status.
common_wrong_answer: A general LLM would likely state that the SEC's 2019 package established a uniform 'best interest' standard that applies to both broker-dealers and investment advisers alike, and would either incorrectly assert that the federal framework preempts state-level fiduciary standards under general Supremacy Clause principles, or incorrectly state that Section 913 of Dodd-Frank mandated a uniform fiduciary standard. The model would likely miss that the Fiduciary Interpretation uses distinct language ('must not place its own interest ahead of its client's interests') from Reg BI's formulation, and would not know that the Fiduciary Interpretation applies to all investment advisers regardless of registration status or retail customer base. Most models would also fail to identify that the Solely Incidental Interpretation specifically acknowledged that broker-dealers may provide 'substantial amounts' of advice under the exclusion.
applicable_standard: SEC Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR § 240.15l-1); SEC Fiduciary Interpretation (IA-5248); SEC Solely Incidental Interpretation (IA-5249); Form CRS (Form ADV Part 3); Section 913(f) of the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act (Pub. L. No. 111-203, § 913, 124 Stat. 1376, 1827-28 (2010)); Investment Advisers Act of 1940 § 202(a)(11); Massachusetts Uniform Securities Act; NASAA Model Rules on fiduciary duty

fact_pattern:
Greenfield Securities, Inc. ('Greenfield') is a broker-dealer registered in Massachusetts and 42 other states, with its principal office in Hartford, Connecticut. Greenfield maintains 15 branch offices in Massachusetts and serves approximately 18,000 retail brokerage customers nationwide. Since 2015, Greenfield has employed a tiered commission schedule for equity transactions, charging a minimum commission of $65 per equity buy or sell transaction for trades below a certain principal threshold. In June 2017, Greenfield's compliance department reviewed its commission schedule and determined that the $65 minimum commission was consistent with industry norms and FINRA markup/markdown guidance under FINRA Rule 2121 and its supplementary material. Greenfield's CCO, Sandra Whitfield, documented this review and concluded that because the firm's minimum commission was below the commonly cited 5% guideline for equity transactions above $1,300 in principal, no changes were necessary.

Between January 2017 and June 2018, Greenfield executed approximately 45,000 low-principal equity transactions (trades under $2,500 in principal) for retail customers, on which the $65 minimum commission was applied. For a significant subset of these trades — roughly 12,000 transactions involving principal amounts under $500 — the effective commission rate exceeded 13%, and in some cases exceeded 30% of the principal amount. Greenfield's financial advisors were not required to seek supervisory approval before executing low-principal trades subject to the minimum commission, and no automated surveillance flagged the effective percentage rates on these small-dollar transactions.

In September 2020, following the implementation of Regulation Best Interest on June 30, 2020, Greenfield updated its policies to require that financial advisors document a cost-benefit analysis for any equity trade where the commission would exceed 5% of the principal amount. However, Greenfield did not retroactively review or remediate the pre-Reg BI low-principal trades from 2017–2018. In March 2023, the Massachusetts Securities Division, acting as a lead state in a multi-state coordinated investigation, opened an inquiry into Greenfield's minimum commission practices. The Division's investigation focused on the period from July 1, 2018, to the present, mirroring the approach used in a contemporaneous enforcement action against another major broker-dealer.

Greenfield's outside counsel, Victor Hargrove of Hargrove & Mills LLP, argued in response to the Division's inquiry that (1) the pre-June 30, 2020 trades were governed only by the suitability standard under FINRA Rule 2111 and the general fairness requirements of FINRA Rule 2121, not Reg BI, and therefore the firm's compliance review in 2017 immunized those trades; and (2) Massachusetts could not reach conduct occurring before July 1, 2018, because any investigation should be limited to the relevant time period established in comparable state enforcement actions. Hargrove further contended that the 2020 adoption of Reg BI represented the first time a specific obligation to evaluate cost relative to principal on small-dollar equity trades was imposed, and that holding Greenfield liable for pre-Reg BI conduct would constitute an impermissible retroactive application of the new standard.

The Massachusetts Securities Division rejected these arguments. The Division pointed to its own statutory and regulatory framework as the basis for the enforcement action, noting that the obligation to charge fair and reasonable commissions predated Reg BI and was independently enforceable under Massachusetts law. The Division also noted that its investigation's relevant time period began on July 1, 2018 — not on the Reg BI effective date — capturing 24 months of pre-Reg BI conduct.
question: Under the Massachusetts Securities Division's approach as reflected in its 2023 consent order against Raymond James (Docket No. E-2023-0041), why does Greenfield's argument that pre-Reg BI conduct cannot be reached fail, and what specific temporal boundary did the Division establish for its investigation that captures conduct predating Reg BI's June 30, 2020 effective date? Additionally, what was the approximate scale of the comparable enforcement action that demonstrates the Division's willingness to pursue unreasonable commission claims for pre-Reg BI periods under state law authority?
correct_answer:
Greenfield's argument fails because the Massachusetts Securities Division's enforcement authority over unreasonable commissions derives from the Massachusetts Uniform Securities Act (Mass. Gen. Laws c. 110A) and its implementing regulations (950 Code Mass. Regs. 10.01-14.413), not from SEC Regulation Best Interest. The consent order in the Raymond James matter (Docket No. E-2023-0041) establishes that the Division's relevant time period ran from approximately July 1, 2018, to the present — a full two years before Reg BI's June 30, 2020 effective date. This demonstrates that the Division considers the obligation to charge fair and reasonable commissions on equity transactions to be an independent state-law requirement that existed well before Reg BI.

The Raymond James consent order specifically found that the respondents charged unreasonable commissions on approximately 270,000 low-principal equity transactions nationwide over the past five years, totaling over $8,250,000. The Division acted as a lead state in a coordinated multi-state investigation, and the enforcement theory was grounded in the state's own statutory framework — not in any federal standard. The tiered commission schedule, including a minimum commission of $75 for certain equity buy and sell transactions, was found to result in unreasonable effective commission rates on low-principal trades regardless of whether Reg BI had been adopted.

Thus, Greenfield cannot shield its July 2018 through June 2020 conduct by arguing that Reg BI had not yet taken effect. The Massachusetts Division's approach explicitly encompasses pre-Reg BI conduct dating to July 1, 2018, and the state's independent authority to police unreasonable commissions under its own securities laws means that the fairness obligation applied throughout the entire relevant time period. The $8.25 million, 270,000-transaction scale of the Raymond James action demonstrates the Division's capacity and willingness to pursue these claims aggressively on a nationwide basis using state-law theories that federal regulators did not independently pursue.
why_adversarial: This question is adversarial because a general LLM would likely focus on the Reg BI effective date (June 30, 2020) as the key temporal boundary and might conclude that pre-Reg BI conduct is harder to reach or that FINRA Rule 2121's 5% markup policy was the governing standard. The correct answer requires knowing the SPECIFIC relevant time period (July 1, 2018) established in the Massachusetts consent order, the exact scale of the enforcement action ($8,250,000 across approximately 270,000 transactions), the specific minimum commission amount ($75), and the fact that Massachusetts pursued this as a state-law theory independent of Reg BI. Without the document, a model would not know the precise temporal starting point or the enforcement action's scale, and would likely incorrectly treat Reg BI's effective date as the dividing line for liability.
common_wrong_answer: A general LLM would likely argue that pre-June 30, 2020 conduct is governed solely by the FINRA suitability standard and FINRA Rule 2121's markup/markdown guidance, and that the key temporal dividing line is Reg BI's effective date. It would likely state that Greenfield's 2017 compliance review documenting adherence to the 5% guideline provides a reasonable defense for pre-Reg BI trades, and might suggest that Massachusetts would need to rely on Reg BI's cost component to establish that low-principal commissions were unreasonable. The model would not know that the Massachusetts Division specifically set July 1, 2018 (not June 30, 2020) as the start of the relevant time period, or that the Raymond James action involved approximately 270,000 transactions and $8.25 million in unreasonable commissions pursued entirely under state law authority.
applicable_standard: Massachusetts Uniform Securities Act, Mass. Gen. Laws c. 110A; 950 Code Mass. Regs. 10.01-14.413; Massachusetts Securities Division Consent Order Docket No. E-2023-0041; SEC Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR § 240.15l-1, effective June 30, 2020); FINRA Rule 2121 (Fair Prices and Commissions); FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability)

fact_pattern:
In January 2020, Greenfield Digital Commodities LLC, a Chicago-based firm, began offering tokenized agricultural commodity contracts to retail investors through a mobile application. These contracts, branded as 'FarmTokens,' purported to give holders exposure to corn and soybean futures prices but were structured as smart contracts on the Ethereum blockchain rather than as traditional futures contracts cleared through a designated clearing organization (DCO). Greenfield was not registered with the CFTC as a futures commission merchant (FCM), nor was it registered with any state securities regulator. By March 2020, Greenfield had approximately 14,000 retail customers across 38 states, with aggregate customer deposits of $47.3 million.

The Illinois Secretary of State's Securities Department opened an investigation in April 2020 after receiving complaints from Illinois residents who lost approximately $2.1 million when Greenfield's smart contracts malfunctioned during the historic negative oil price event. The state regulator alleged that the FarmTokens constituted unregistered securities under Illinois law and also constituted commodity interests that fell within federal jurisdiction. Simultaneously, the CFTC's Division of Enforcement began a parallel investigation, asserting that FarmTokens were swaps or futures subject to CFTC jurisdiction under the Commodity Exchange Act (CEA).

Greenfield's counsel argued that because the CFTC had undergone an extensive self-assessment of its regulatory framework for the IMF's 2020 Financial Sector Assessment Program (FSAP), any gaps in coverage of novel digital commodity products should be attributed to the federal regulator's acknowledged limitations, and that state regulators should therefore be preempted from acting. Greenfield specifically pointed to the CFTC's own FSAP self-assessment, which covered only a subset of the IOSCO Principles and explicitly disclaimed that its responses constituted rules, regulations, or statements of the CFTC.

The Illinois regulator countered that the CFTC's FSAP self-assessment was a non-binding staff document that could not serve as a basis for federal preemption, and that the state retained concurrent jurisdiction over products that might constitute both securities under state law and commodity interests under federal law. The NASAA Model Rules on digital assets, still in development, had not yet been finalized. The question of whether a state enforcement action could proceed against a hybrid digital commodity product—where the federal regulator had explicitly disclaimed the binding nature of its own regulatory self-assessment and the assessment covered only a limited subset of international regulatory principles—remained unresolved.

Greenfield also raised the argument that because the CFTC's self-assessment was prepared 'solely for purposes of the IMF's 2020 Financial Sector Assessment Program (FSAP) mission in the United States,' any regulatory gap identified through that process could not be used by state regulators to justify expanded state jurisdiction. The firm contended that the CFTC's assessment of Principles 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 9, 24-28, 29-32, and 33-37 demonstrated comprehensive federal oversight of market intermediaries, trading venues, and direct electronic access providers, leaving no room for state action.
question: Given that the CFTC's July 2019 FSAP self-assessment explicitly states it covers only a specific subset of IOSCO Principles and contains a detailed disclaimer about its non-binding nature, can Greenfield successfully invoke the self-assessment's coverage of Principles 29-32 (which the document limits to 'market intermediaries that are direct participants in trading venues, providers of direct electronic access to such venues and/or first tier direct electronic access clients, and operators of trading venues') to argue that federal oversight is comprehensive enough to preempt Illinois's state securities enforcement action against its tokenized commodity contracts?
correct_answer:
No. Greenfield's argument fails on multiple grounds rooted in the specific text of the CFTC's FSAP self-assessment. First, the self-assessment document itself contains an express disclaimer stating that the responses 'are not rules, regulations, or statements of the CFTC' and that 'the CFTC has neither approved nor disapproved these responses.' The document further warns that its contents 'should not be deemed to constitute interpretive advice by the staff of the CFTC or be used or relied upon for legal purposes.' A document that explicitly disclaims legal authority cannot serve as the basis for a federal preemption argument, which requires affirmative federal regulatory occupation of a field.

Second, and critically, the self-assessment's coverage of Principles 29-32 is expressly limited in scope to 'market intermediaries that are direct participants in trading venues, providers of direct electronic access to such venues and/or first tier direct electronic access clients, and operators of trading venues.' Greenfield's FarmTokens were offered directly to retail investors via a mobile application, not through a designated trading venue, and Greenfield was not a registered market intermediary or operator of a trading venue. The very specificity of the CFTC's self-assessed scope under Principles 29-32 demonstrates that Greenfield's activities would fall outside the subset of regulatory coverage the CFTC chose to self-assess for FSAP purposes.

Third, the CEA's savings clause (7 U.S.C. § 16(e)) generally preserves state jurisdiction over fraud-based claims, and the CFTC's self-assessment—prepared 'solely for purposes of the IMF's 2020 Financial Sector Assessment Program'—cannot expand the preemptive scope of federal commodity law beyond what Congress enacted. Illinois retains authority under state securities laws to pursue unregistered offerings, and the CFTC's FSAP document, which explicitly covers only a subset of IOSCO Principles and disclaims binding effect, provides no basis for preemption. The state enforcement action may proceed concurrently with any CFTC action.
why_adversarial: This question requires knowledge of three specific details from the actual CFTC FSAP self-assessment document that a general LLM would not know: (1) the exact disclaimer language stating the responses are 'not rules, regulations, or statements of the CFTC' and should not be 'used or relied upon for legal purposes'; (2) the specific limitation on Principles 29-32 coverage to 'market intermediaries that are direct participants in trading venues, providers of direct electronic access to such venues and/or first tier direct electronic access clients, and operators of trading venues'; and (3) the document's express statement that it was prepared 'solely for purposes of the IMF's 2020 Financial Sector Assessment Program.' Without knowing these precise textual limitations, a model might reason generally about federal preemption of state commodity regulation and conclude that CFTC oversight could preempt state action—the opposite of the correct answer.
common_wrong_answer: A general LLM would likely analyze this as a straightforward federal preemption question and conclude that because the CFTC has broad jurisdiction over commodity futures and swaps under the CEA, and because the CFTC conducted a comprehensive self-assessment covering market intermediaries and trading venues, the federal regulatory framework is sufficiently comprehensive to preempt state securities enforcement actions against tokenized commodity products. The model would likely apply general CEA preemption principles (7 U.S.C. § 2(a)(1)(A)) without recognizing that the CFTC's FSAP self-assessment is explicitly non-binding, covers only a limited subset of principles, and narrows Principles 29-32 to specific categories of market participants that would not include a mobile-app-based retail token issuer.
applicable_standard: CFTC FSAP Self-Assessment (July 31, 2019); IOSCO Objectives and Principles of Securities Regulation (Principles 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 9, 24-28, 29-32 (limited scope), 33-37); Commodity Exchange Act § 2(a)(1)(A) (7 U.S.C. § 2(a)(1)(A)); CEA savings clause (7 U.S.C. § 16(e)); Illinois Securities Law of 1953 (815 ILCS 5/); NASAA Model Rules; Uniform Securities Act

fact_pattern:
In March 2023, Oakwood Capital Partners, a FINRA-registered broker-dealer headquartered in Columbus, Ohio, recommended that its client Margaret Townsend, a 68-year-old retiree with a liquid net worth of $425,000 and annual income of $62,000, invest $95,000 in NorthStar Healthcare REIT II, a non-traded REIT registered under Regulation A+ and offered through a prospectus reviewed by the Ohio Division of Securities. Oakwood's registered representative, Daniel Firth, completed the firm's standard Reg BI disclosure obligations—delivering a Form CRS, providing the applicable relationship summary, and documenting that the recommendation was in Margaret's best interest based on her stated investment objectives of income generation and capital preservation.

The non-traded REIT's sponsor, NorthStar Capital Management LLC (an SEC-registered investment adviser that also served as the external adviser to the REIT), prepared the offering circular, which included a suitability section specifying minimum net income and net worth standards for investors. The offering circular did not include any concentration limit for investors. NorthStar Capital Management had contracted with Pinnacle Fund Services, Inc., an independent transfer agent and administrator, to process subscription agreements and verify investor eligibility. Pinnacle processed Margaret's subscription without flagging any issues.

After the investment, Margaret's total allocation to non-traded REITs (including two prior positions totaling $55,000) reached $150,000, or approximately 35.3% of her liquid net worth. Six months later, NorthStar Healthcare REIT II suspended distributions and announced an estimated NAV decline of 38%, reducing Margaret's position to approximately $58,900. Margaret filed a complaint with the Ohio Division of Securities.

The Ohio Division opened an investigation and discovered that the REIT Guidelines had been revised in late 2022 to include a new standardized concentration limit provision. Ohio had adopted the revised NASAA REIT Guidelines, including the new concentration limit, as part of its state merit review standards. The concentration limit provision caps investor exposure to non-traded REITs at a specified percentage of the investor's liquid net worth, and Margaret's aggregate position clearly exceeded this threshold at the time of the Oakwood recommendation.

Oakwood argues that it complied with federal Reg BI and FINRA Rule 2111, and that any state-level concentration limit is preempted. NorthStar Capital Management contends that as the sponsor and external adviser, it relied on the broker-dealer's compliance with applicable suitability and conduct standards. Pinnacle Fund Services asserts it had no obligation to monitor concentration limits, only to verify minimum income and net worth eligibility as stated in the offering circular. The Ohio Division is considering enforcement action and weighing which parties are liable under the revised NASAA REIT Guidelines.
question: Under the proposed revisions to the NASAA Statement of Policy Regarding Real Estate Investment Trusts (as described in the July 2022 Request for Public Comment), which of the four parties—Oakwood Capital Partners (the broker-dealer), NorthStar Capital Management (the sponsor/external adviser), Pinnacle Fund Services (the transfer agent), or Daniel Firth (the registered representative)—bears primary liability for the concentration limit violation, and specifically: (a) what new provision in the revised REIT Guidelines creates the concentration limit obligation, (b) how does the revised Guidelines' dual incorporation of both the suitability standard AND Reg BI best interest standard affect the broker-dealer's defense that federal Reg BI compliance is sufficient, and (c) does the fact that the offering circular's suitability section did not include the concentration limit relieve any of the parties given NASAA's proposed revision framework?
correct_answer:
Under the proposed revisions to the NASAA REIT Guidelines described in the July 2022 Request for Public Comment, the broker-dealer (Oakwood Capital Partners) and its associated person (Daniel Firth) bear primary liability. The key provision is Proposed Revision (3)—the addition of a new standardized concentration limit to the suitability section of the REIT Guidelines. This is one of the four enumerated primary revisions, and it operates at the state merit review level, meaning it governs the terms under which non-traded REITs may be offered and sold in states that have adopted the NASAA Guidelines. The concentration limit is embedded in the suitability section of the Guidelines, which directly governs the conduct of persons selling or recommending the program's shares—i.e., the broker-dealer and its registered representatives.

Critically, Proposed Revision (1) supplements the existing suitability standard with references to the new Reg BI best interest conduct standard. The July 2022 Request explicitly states that the revision 'formally incorporat[es] into the guidelines this new conduct standard' alongside the existing suitability framework. This means the revised Guidelines do not treat Reg BI as a replacement for state-level suitability and concentration requirements—they layer federal Reg BI on top of the NASAA suitability provisions, including the new concentration limit. Oakwood's defense that federal Reg BI compliance is sufficient therefore fails: the revised NASAA Guidelines explicitly contemplate a dual-standard regime where Reg BI compliance is necessary but not sufficient, because the state-level concentration limit is an additional, independent requirement within the suitability section that Reg BI does not address.

The sponsor (NorthStar) and transfer agent (Pinnacle) have limited but not zero exposure. The offering circular's suitability section is expected to reflect the NASAA Guidelines' requirements, including the new concentration limit, as a condition of state registration or merit review approval. If Ohio adopted the revised Guidelines including Revision (3), then the offering circular should have been updated to include the concentration limit. NorthStar, as the sponsor who prepared the offering circular, could face secondary liability for failing to include the concentration limit in the prospectus suitability section. However, the primary conduct obligation falls on the selling broker-dealer and its representative, because the REIT Guidelines' suitability section—including the concentration limit—expressly governs 'the standard of conduct that applies to persons selling or recommending the program's shares.' Pinnacle's defense is strongest: as transfer agent, it processes subscriptions based on eligibility criteria stated in the offering circular, and concentration monitoring is outside its contractual and regulatory scope under the NASAA framework.
why_adversarial: This question requires knowledge of three specific details from the July 2022 NASAA Request for Public Comment that a general LLM would not know: (1) that the proposed revisions include a NEW standardized concentration limit as a distinct provision added to the suitability section (Revision 3), (2) that Revision 1 supplements (not replaces) the suitability standard with Reg BI references—creating a layered dual-standard framework rather than preempting state requirements, and (3) that the suitability section of the REIT Guidelines governs 'persons selling or recommending the program's shares,' which channels primary liability to the broker-dealer and its associated persons rather than the sponsor or transfer agent. A general LLM would likely default to standard Reg BI preemption arguments or distribute liability evenly without understanding the specific NASAA framework.
common_wrong_answer: A general LLM would likely argue that Reg BI preempts state-level concentration requirements under federal supremacy principles, and would either (a) conclude that Oakwood's Reg BI compliance provides a complete defense, or (b) assign primary liability to NorthStar as the sponsor/adviser under a fiduciary standard theory, or (c) distribute liability equally among all parties. The model would not know that the NASAA Guidelines specifically layer the concentration limit on top of Reg BI rather than being displaced by it, and would not correctly identify that the suitability section's language specifically targets selling brokers rather than sponsors or transfer agents.
applicable_standard: NASAA Statement of Policy Regarding Real Estate Investment Trusts (proposed revisions July 2022): Revision (1) (incorporation of Reg BI alongside suitability standard); Revision (2) (updated net income/net worth thresholds); Revision (3) (new standardized concentration limit in suitability section); Revision (4) (prohibition on using gross offering proceeds for distributions); SEC Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR § 240.15l-1); FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability); Ohio Division of Securities merit review standards incorporating NASAA Guidelines

fact_pattern:
In January 2023, the State Securities Division of Arkandale (a fictional U.S. state that has adopted NASAA Model Rules and also incorporated by reference the IOSCO Objectives and Principles of Securities Regulation as interpretive guidance for cross-border enforcement matters) opened an investigation into Meridian Capital Partners LLC, a state-registered investment adviser with $85 million in assets under management. Meridian had been marketing a series of collective investment schemes — structured as limited partnerships — to approximately 340 retail investors across Arkandale and two neighboring states. The schemes invested primarily in offshore derivative instruments through a Cayman Islands-domiciled feeder fund managed by an entity called Trident Offshore Management Ltd.

The Arkandale Securities Division's enforcement chief, Sandra Halloran, suspected that Meridian had failed to disclose material conflicts of interest in its marketing materials and had misrepresented the fund's risk profile. Halloran's team also believed that approximately $12 million in investor funds had been diverted to accounts controlled by Meridian's principal, David Kessler, through a series of intermediary entities in Singapore. To trace the funds, Halloran needed transaction records and account statements from both the Cayman and Singaporean entities.

Halloran's office sent formal requests to the Monetary Authority of Singapore and the Cayman Islands Monetary Authority seeking non-public transactional information, account holder data, and internal compliance records from Trident Offshore Management Ltd. and the Singaporean intermediaries. The Arkandale division justified these requests by citing the IOSCO Objectives and Principles of Securities Regulation, which Arkandale had incorporated into its regulatory framework as interpretive authority for cross-border cooperation.

The Cayman Islands regulator responded that it would share certain public information but questioned the legal basis for sharing non-public information with a sub-national regulator. Singapore's regulator similarly asked for clarification on the specific IOSCO principles that Arkandale was relying upon and whether the principles distinguished between public and non-public information sharing obligations. David Kessler's defense counsel, meanwhile, filed a motion to quash any evidence obtained from the foreign regulators, arguing that the IOSCO principles do not create binding obligations and that the Arkandale division had failed to comply with the specific procedural framework set forth in those principles.

Halloran's office needs to respond to both the foreign regulators and Kessler's motion. The response must identify the precise IOSCO principles governing information sharing between regulators and explain whether those principles distinguish between public and non-public information in the context of regulatory cooperation.
question: Under the IOSCO Objectives and Principles of Securities Regulation (May 2003), which specific numbered principles address information sharing between regulators, and critically, do those principles draw a distinction between sharing public versus non-public information — and if so, which principle(s) specifically reference non-public information sharing? Additionally, how many total principles does the document enumerate, and into how many categories are they organized?
correct_answer:
The IOSCO Objectives and Principles of Securities Regulation (May 2003) enumerates exactly 30 principles organized into eight categories. The principles specifically addressing information sharing between regulators fall under Category D, 'Principles for Cooperation in Regulation,' which contains Principles 11, 12, and 13.

Critically, the IOSCO framework does explicitly distinguish between public and non-public information. Principle 11 states that 'the regulator should have authority to share both public and non-public information with domestic and foreign counterparts.' Principle 12 further specifies that 'regulators should establish information sharing mechanisms that set out when and how they will share both public and non-public information with their domestic and foreign counterparts.' Both Principles 11 and 12 use the precise phrase 'both public and non-public information,' making an explicit textual distinction. Principle 13 addresses the broader obligation that 'the regulatory system should allow for assistance to be provided to foreign regulators who need to make inquiries in the discharge of their functions and exercise of their powers,' but does not itself use the public/non-public distinction.

Therefore, Halloran's office can cite Principles 11 and 12 specifically in responding to both the Cayman and Singaporean regulators, because those principles expressly contemplate the sharing of non-public information. The Cayman regulator's hesitation about sharing non-public information is directly addressed by Principle 11's requirement that regulators should have the authority to share non-public information. However, Kessler's counsel is correct that the IOSCO principles are not themselves binding legal instruments — they are standards and objectives that member jurisdictions commit to implement through their own legal frameworks. The principles do not create independent enforcement authority but serve as interpretive guidance where incorporated by reference, as Arkandale has done.
why_adversarial: This question requires precise knowledge of the IOSCO document's exact structure: 30 principles in 8 categories, and the specific language of Principles 11, 12, and 13 under Category D. A general LLM would likely know that IOSCO has principles about cooperation but would not know the exact numbering, that there are precisely 30 principles in 8 categories, or that Principles 11 and 12 both specifically use the phrase 'both public and non-public information' while Principle 13 does not. The distinction between which of the three cooperation principles explicitly reference non-public information versus which do not is a granular textual detail that requires access to the actual document.
common_wrong_answer: A general LLM would likely state that IOSCO has principles about information sharing and cooperation but would either guess incorrectly at the number of total principles (often citing 38 principles from the post-2010 revision), misidentify the number of categories, or fail to correctly identify that Principles 11 AND 12 both explicitly reference 'non-public information' while Principle 13 does not use that specific terminology. Many models would also incorrectly assert that all three cooperation principles (11, 12, and 13) equally address the public/non-public distinction, or would cite the wrong edition of the IOSCO principles entirely.
applicable_standard: IOSCO Objectives and Principles of Securities Regulation (May 2003), Principles 11-13 (Category D: Principles for Cooperation in Regulation); NASAA Model Rules (as adopted by jurisdiction incorporating IOSCO principles as interpretive guidance); Uniform Securities Act provisions on cross-border regulatory cooperation

fact_pattern:
In early 2024, Pinnacle Wealth Partners LLC, a small investment advisory firm based in Austin, Texas, managing approximately $85 million in client assets, received notice from the Texas State Securities Board that it was being examined as part of a routine state regulatory review. The firm's principal, Gerald Harmon, had been registered as a state-registered investment adviser since 2019. During the examination, state examiners discovered that Pinnacle had failed to update its Form ADV Part 2A brochure for two consecutive annual amendment periods, had not conducted annual compliance reviews as required, and had charged performance-based fees to three non-qualified clients with account values ranging from $45,000 to $120,000. Additionally, one of Pinnacle's two investment adviser representatives had let his Series 65 qualification lapse for eight months during 2023 before quietly re-qualifying.

Harmon's defense counsel argued that because Texas was experiencing a net increase in state-registered investment advisers — one of only five states to see growth during 2022-2023 — the Texas State Securities Board's examination resources were necessarily stretched thinner, and that the Board's enforcement priorities should focus on outright fraud rather than technical compliance deficiencies. Counsel further argued that Pinnacle's violations were the exact type of minor, non-fraud deficiencies commonly found through routine examinations and typically resolved through deficiency letters rather than formal enforcement action.

Concurrently, a nearly identical firm, Lakeshore Advisory Group LLC, based in Ohio and managing $78 million, was found by Ohio regulators to have committed the same violations — outdated ADV, no annual compliance review, improper performance fees, and a lapsed representative qualification. Ohio, however, saw a net decrease in its state-registered IA population during the same period. Ohio's regulator issued a formal cease-and-desist order and imposed a $25,000 fine against Lakeshore.

Both firms pointed to the NASAA 2024 Investment Adviser Section Annual Report's data showing that total state-registered IAs nationwide experienced a net decrease of 166 firms from 2022 to 2023 (from approximately 17,063 to 16,897), while total state-registered IA registrations (including out-of-state) actually saw a net increase of 280 registrations during the same period. Both firms argued this divergence suggested a regulatory environment in flux that counseled leniency.

The Texas Securities Board ultimately resolved the matter with a deficiency letter and no formal enforcement action, while Ohio proceeded with full enforcement. Both outcomes were reached in states governed by substantially similar provisions of the Uniform Securities Act.
question: Given the NASAA 2024 IA Section Report data showing that the total number of state-registered investment advisers decreased by 166 firms nationwide from 2022 to 2023 while total state-registered IA registrations (including out-of-state) simultaneously increased by 280, and given that Texas was specifically identified as one of the top five states experiencing an increase in state-registered IAs (gaining 14 home-state IAs), how does this specific statistical divergence undermine or support Harmon's argument that Texas's growing IA population justified leniency, and what counterintuitive conclusion does the data support about the relationship between state IA population growth and enforcement intensity?
correct_answer:
The NASAA 2024 IA Section Report reveals a counterintuitive statistical reality that actually undermines Harmon's argument. While the total number of home-state registered IAs decreased by 166 nationwide (from approximately 17,063 to 16,897 as of December 31, 2023), total state-registered IA registrations including out-of-state registrations increased by 280 (to 27,796). This divergence means that while fewer firms existed overall, those remaining firms were registering in more jurisdictions — expanding their multi-state footprints. Texas specifically was identified as having 4,628 total state-registered IAs (including out-of-state) versus only 1,400 home-state IAs, meaning Texas regulators oversee more than three times as many IAs as are domiciled there.

This data actually supports the counterintuitive conclusion that Texas's position as the #1 state for total IA registrations (4,628) — despite being only #2 for home-state IAs (1,400) — means Texas regulators face a disproportionately large supervisory burden from out-of-state advisers registering into Texas. Harmon's argument that Texas's modest home-state growth of 14 IAs stretched resources is undermined by the fact that the real supervisory challenge comes from the 3,228 out-of-state IAs registered in Texas. The net decrease in nationwide home-state IAs combined with the net increase in total registrations indicates firms are consolidating while expanding geographically, which actually increases the complexity of state oversight rather than diminishing it.

The counterintuitive outcome is that the deficiency-letter resolution in Texas — seemingly lenient — may actually reflect a rational triage decision by a regulator overwhelmed not by home-state growth but by the massive influx of out-of-state registrations. Ohio's stricter enforcement, by contrast, occurred in a state with a shrinking IA population (only 396 home-state IAs) where regulators had proportionally more bandwidth per registrant. The data suggests that enforcement intensity may be inversely correlated with total registration burden, not positively correlated with home-state IA growth as Harmon argued.
why_adversarial: This question requires knowledge of specific numerical data points unique to the NASAA 2024 IA Section Report: the precise net decrease of 166 home-state IAs, the simultaneous net increase of 280 total registrations, Texas's specific ranking as #1 in total registrations (4,628) versus #2 in home-state IAs (1,400), and the exact growth figure of 14 for Texas. A general LLM would not know the specific divergence between home-state IA counts and total registration counts, would not know that Texas has more than 3x as many total registrants as home-state IAs, and would likely default to the intuitive but incorrect conclusion that growing IA populations mean more enforcement rather than recognizing the resource-strain dynamic revealed by the data. The counterintuitive element — that a state with a growing IA population may enforce less aggressively precisely because of that growth — can only be derived from the specific statistical relationships in the document.
common_wrong_answer: A general LLM would likely argue that Texas's growing IA population would lead to increased enforcement intensity (more advisers = more examinations = stricter outcomes), and that Harmon's argument about stretched resources is irrelevant because states have an obligation to enforce regardless of population size. The model would probably not recognize the critical divergence between home-state IAs and total registrations, would not know the specific 4,628 vs. 1,400 Texas figures, and would likely conclude that both Texas and Ohio should have reached the same enforcement outcome under the Uniform Securities Act. The model would miss the counterintuitive conclusion that the statistical data actually supports different enforcement outcomes in different states based on registration burden ratios.
applicable_standard: NASAA 2024 Investment Adviser Section Annual Report (2023-2024 data); Uniform Securities Act provisions on state IA registration and enforcement; NASAA Model Rules on IA compliance obligations; Individual state securities board enforcement discretion under state Blue Sky laws; Form ADV Parts 1 and 2A filing and amendment requirements; NASAA coordinated examination program standards

fact_pattern:
Meridian Wealth Partners LLC is a federal covered investment adviser registered with the SEC, managing $3.2 billion in assets across 14 states. On March 3, 2024, Meridian's senior portfolio manager, Danielle Ostrowski, received a phone call from long-time client Gerald Huntington, a retired aerospace engineer with a $4.7 million discretionary portfolio. During the call, Huntington verbally authorized Ostrowski to begin rebalancing his portfolio by liquidating approximately $800,000 in long-dated Treasury bonds and reallocating to a mix of investment-grade corporate bonds and dividend-paying equities. Huntington stated he would sign whatever paperwork was needed 'when he got around to it.'

Ostrowski immediately began executing trades on March 4, 2024, selling $812,000 in Treasuries and purchasing a diversified basket of securities consistent with Huntington's stated objectives. Between March 4 and March 14, she executed a total of 11 transactions in the account, all consistent with the rebalancing instructions Huntington had given orally. On March 15, Ostrowski emailed Huntington a written discretionary authorization form. Huntington signed and returned it on March 22, 2024 — 13 business days after the first trade was placed on March 4.

The state of Colorado, where Huntington resides, subsequently initiated an enforcement investigation into Meridian's practices. Colorado has adopted the NASAA Model Rule USA 2002 502(b) and applies it to federal covered investment advisers to the extent the conduct alleged is fraudulent, deceptive, or as otherwise permitted by NSMIA. Meridian's compliance counsel argues that as a federal covered adviser, Meridian is subject solely to the SEC's regulations under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 and Rule 206(4)-2 thereunder, and that Colorado lacks jurisdiction to impose the specific discretionary authority documentation requirements found in the NASAA Model Rule.

The SEC's Advisers Act and Rule 206(4)-7 require advisers to adopt and implement written compliance policies reasonably designed to prevent violations, and SEC guidance generally requires written discretionary authority but does not specify a fixed business-day deadline for converting oral authority to written form. Meridian's own compliance manual states that written discretionary authorization should be obtained 'promptly' after oral authorization but does not define a specific number of days.

Colorado's securities division contends that (1) exercising discretionary authority without timely written authorization is inherently deceptive conduct within the meaning of NSMIA's fraud carve-out, enabling the state to reach a federal covered adviser, and (2) the specific 10-business-day deadline in the NASAA Model Rule was breached because the written authorization was not obtained until the 13th business day after the first discretionary trade.
question: Under NASAA Model Rule USA 2002 502(b)(b), what is the precise deadline for obtaining written discretionary authority after the first transaction placed under oral authorization, and does the rule's application to a federal covered investment adviser like Meridian require a showing of fraudulent or deceptive conduct under NSMIA — or does the 10-business-day discretionary authority provision apply independently? Specifically, did Ostrowski violate the rule, and can Colorado enforce it against Meridian given its federal covered status?
correct_answer:
Under NASAA Model Rule USA 2002 502(b)(b), an investment adviser must obtain written discretionary authority from the client within ten (10) business days after the date of the first transaction placed pursuant to oral discretionary authority. The only exception is where the discretionary authority relates solely to the price at which, or the time when, an order involving a definite amount of a specified security shall be executed, or both. Here, Ostrowski's oral authority covered the full scope of what to buy and sell — not merely price or timing of a definite order — so the exception does not apply. The written authorization was obtained on the 13th business day after the March 4 first trade, which exceeds the 10-business-day deadline by three business days. This constitutes a clear violation of the rule's text.

Critically, the preamble to Rule USA 2002 502(b) explicitly states that its provisions 'apply to federal covered investment advisers to the extent that the conduct alleged is fraudulent, deceptive, or as otherwise permitted by the National Securities Markets Improvement Act of 1996.' Colorado's enforcement theory depends on characterizing the failure to timely obtain written discretionary authorization as fraudulent or deceptive conduct — not merely a technical paperwork violation. The rule itself classifies exercising discretionary authority without timely written authorization as one of the enumerated forms of 'prohibited fraudulent, deceptive, or manipulative conduct,' which strengthens Colorado's position. Because the NASAA Model Rule frames all of subsection (b)'s enumerated prohibitions — including the discretionary authority provision — as species of 'fraudulent, deceptive, or manipulative conduct,' Colorado can argue this characterization satisfies NSMIA's fraud carve-out for state jurisdiction over federal covered advisers.

Meridian's defense that the SEC does not impose a specific business-day deadline is beside the point.
