However, Greenfield's in-house counsel, Marcus Webb, argued that because the company's public float is $560 million — well above the $250 million threshold — there may be a transition provision that overrides the exclusion.

The company also needs to determine the correct filing deadline for its Form 10-K: 60 days after fiscal year-end (as applicable to large accelerated filers), 75 days (as applicable to accelerated filers), or 90 days (as applicable to non-accelerated filers). The EY guidance document on 2023 Form 10-K filings specifically addresses the interplay between accelerated filer status, SRC status, and the ICFR attestation requirement, including the exit provisions and transition rules that apply when a company moves between these categories.
question: Under the SEC's 2020 amendments to the accelerated filer definition as discussed in the EY 2023 Form 10-K guidance (specifically Sections 2.1.2 through 2.1.5), does Greenfield Dynamics qualify as an accelerated filer for its fiscal year 2023 Form 10-K, and if not, what is the specific mechanism by which it is excluded — and how does this exclusion resolve the apparent conflict between the SRC exemption from Section 404(b) ICFR auditor attestation and the accelerated filer requirement to include it? Additionally, what is Greenfield's correct Form 10-K filing deadline?
correct_answer:
Under the SEC's 2020 amendments to the accelerated filer definition, which are addressed in Sections 2.1.2 and 2.1.5 of the EY 2023 Form 10-K guidance, Greenfield Dynamics does NOT qualify as an accelerated filer despite its $560 million public float. The 2020 amendments specifically revised Rule 12b-2 to exclude from the accelerated filer definition any issuer that (1) qualifies as an SRC and (2) had annual revenues of less than $100 million in the most recently completed fiscal year. Greenfield meets both conditions: it qualifies as an SRC (public float below $700 million and revenues below $100 million satisfy the SRC revenue test), and its revenues of $82 million are below the $100 million threshold. Therefore, the exclusion applies and Greenfield is classified as a non-accelerated filer.

This exclusion directly resolves the rule conflict between the SRC exemption from Section 404(b) and the accelerated filer's obligation to include the ICFR auditor attestation. Because Greenfield is excluded from accelerated filer status entirely, there is no conflict: as a non-accelerated filer that is also an SRC, Greenfield is exempt from the Section 404(b) auditor attestation requirement. The EY guidance in Section 2.1.5 specifically discusses the transition between accelerated and SRC status and the consequent ICFR attestation requirement, confirming that the 2020 amendments were designed precisely to prevent low-revenue SRCs from being swept into accelerated filer status solely on the basis of public float and thereby being subjected to the costly 404(b) attestation requirement.

As a non-accelerated filer, Greenfield's Form 10-K filing deadline is 90 days after fiscal year-end — i.e., March 30, 2024 (or the next business day if that falls on a weekend or holiday) — rather than the 75-day deadline for accelerated filers or the 60-day deadline for large accelerated filers, as discussed in Section 2.1 of the guidance.
why_adversarial: This question requires specific knowledge of how the EY 2023 Form 10-K guidance document organizes and explains the interplay between the accelerated filer definition (Section 2.1.2), the non-accelerated filer determination (Section 2.1.3), exit provisions (Section 2.1.4), and the transition between accelerated and SRC status regarding ICFR attestation (Section 2.1.5). A general LLM would know about the 2020 amendments at a high level but would likely not know the specific section-by-section structure of this EY guidance or how it frames the conflict resolution. The document's treatment of the exit provisions and transition rules — which are distinct subsections — is critical to understanding when and how a company transitions out of accelerated filer status. Without access to the document, a model might incorrectly conclude that Greenfield's $560 million public float overrides the SRC exclusion or that some transition period applies.
common_wrong_answer: A general LLM would likely state that Greenfield qualifies as an accelerated filer because its $560 million public float exceeds the $75 million threshold, and would then attempt to resolve the SRC vs. accelerated filer conflict by noting the SRC exemption from 404(b) as a standalone carve-out rather than recognizing that the 2020 amendments removed Greenfield from accelerated filer status entirely. The model might say Greenfield is an accelerated filer that also happens to be an SRC and is therefore exempt from 404(b) while still having a 75-day filing deadline — missing the point that the revenue-based exclusion from the accelerated filer definition changes the filing deadline to 90 days as well.
applicable_standard: Exchange Act Rule 12b-2 (accelerated filer definition, as amended in 2020); SEC Release No. 34-88365 (March 2020 amendments); Sarbanes-Oxley Act Section 404(b); Regulation S-K Item 10(f) (SRC definition); Exchange Act Rules 13a-10, 15d-10 (Form 10-K filing deadlines); EY 2023 Form 10-K guidance Sections 2.1.2, 2.1.3, 2.1.4, 2.1.5

fact_pattern:
Ridgecrest Capital Partners LLC is an exempt reporting adviser (ERA) based in Denver, Colorado, with approximately $120 million in assets under management across three private funds. In January 2025, Ridgecrest's Chief Compliance Officer, Sandra Whitfield, is reviewing the firm's anti-money laundering framework following the SEC and FinCEN joint proposed rulemaking issued on May 13, 2024 (File No. S7-2024-02). Ridgecrest has historically operated under the assumption that, as an ERA rather than a fully registered investment adviser, it falls outside the scope of most SEC compliance obligations, including customer identification programs.

Whitfield consults with outside counsel at Barton & Slade LLP, who advises that the proposed CIP rule would require Ridgecrest to implement procedures for verifying the identity of each customer 'to the extent reasonable and practicable' and to maintain records of customer identity information including name, address, and other identifying information. Whitfield is concerned because Ridgecrest's three funds accept investments from both domestic high-net-worth individuals and several foreign family office vehicles domiciled in the Cayman Islands.

Ridgecrest's current onboarding procedures collect investor names and addresses but do not include a formal identity verification protocol or systematic recordkeeping of documents used to verify identity. Whitfield argues to Ridgecrest's managing partners that because the firm is merely an ERA — not a full SEC-registered investment adviser — the proposed CIP rule should not apply to it. She points to the general principle that ERAs have a lighter regulatory burden than RIAs under the Advisers Act.

One of the managing partners, David Kowalski, pushes back, noting that he read a KPMG summary of SEC Division of Investment Management updates from September 2024 that seemed to suggest the proposed CIP rule has a specific scope provision. He asks Whitfield to confirm exactly which categories of investment advisers the proposed rule would cover.

Whitfield also raises the question of whether the proposed rule's obligations differ materially from existing Bank Secrecy Act CIP requirements applicable to broker-dealers, and whether the standard of verification — 'to the extent reasonable and practicable' — creates a lower threshold for ERAs compared to RIAs. She wonders whether ERAs were deliberately included or whether the rule targets only SEC-registered investment advisers.
question: Under the joint SEC/FinCEN proposed rulemaking on Customer Identification Programs issued May 13, 2024 (File No. S7-2024-02), as described in the September 2024 SEC Division of Investment Management Update, which specific categories of investment advisers would be subject to the proposed CIP obligations? Would Ridgecrest Capital Partners, as an exempt reporting adviser, fall within or outside the scope of the proposed rule?
correct_answer:
According to the September 2024 SEC Division of Investment Management Update summarizing the joint SEC/FinCEN proposed rulemaking (File No. S7-2024-02), the proposed CIP rule would apply to both SEC-registered investment advisers (RIAs) AND exempt reporting advisers (ERAs). The document explicitly states the rule is 'Applicable to: RIAs and ERAs,' making clear that the scope is not limited to fully registered advisers.

Therefore, Ridgecrest Capital Partners LLC, despite being an exempt reporting adviser rather than a full SEC-registered investment adviser, would fall squarely within the scope of the proposed CIP obligations. Whitfield's assumption that ERAs carry a lighter regulatory burden and would be excluded from CIP requirements is incorrect with respect to this specific proposed rule. The proposed rule deliberately extends CIP obligations to ERAs as part of the effort to 'prevent illicit finance activity involving the customers of investment advisers by strengthening the anti-money laundering/countering the financing of terrorism (AML/CFT) framework for the investment adviser sector.'

The proposed rule would require Ridgecrest to implement a CIP that includes procedures for (1) verifying the identity of each customer to the extent reasonable and practicable, and (2) maintaining records of the information used to verify a customer's identity, including name, address, and other identifying information. The 'reasonable and practicable' standard applies uniformly — the document does not describe a differentiated or lower threshold for ERAs compared to RIAs. Ridgecrest's current onboarding procedures, which collect names and addresses but lack formal identity verification protocols and systematic recordkeeping of verification documents, would need to be substantially enhanced if the rule is finalized as proposed.
why_adversarial: This question is adversarial because the specific inclusion of exempt reporting advisers (ERAs) within the scope of the proposed CIP rule is a precise detail stated in the document's 'Applicable to' field. A general LLM would likely reason that ERAs, by their nature as 'exempt' advisers with reduced regulatory obligations under the Advisers Act, would not be covered by a new CIP requirement. The conventional understanding is that ERAs have a much lighter compliance burden than RIAs. The explicit inclusion of ERAs in this particular proposed rule is counterintuitive and requires knowledge of the specific document language — specifically the 'Applicable to: RIAs and ERAs' designation — rather than general reasoning about the regulatory treatment of exempt reporting advisers.
common_wrong_answer: A general LLM would likely answer that the proposed CIP rule applies only to SEC-registered investment advisers (RIAs) and that Ridgecrest, as an exempt reporting adviser, would fall outside the scope of the proposed rule. The model would reason that ERAs are 'exempt' from most SEC registration requirements under Section 203(l) or 203(m) of the Advisers Act and therefore would logically be excluded from new compliance obligations like CIP requirements. The model might cite the general principle that ERAs are subject to limited SEC oversight and a reduced set of regulatory obligations, leading it to conclude Whitfield's position is correct.
applicable_standard: Joint SEC/FinCEN Proposed Rulemaking, File No. S7-2024-02 (May 13, 2024); Bank Secrecy Act CIP requirements; Investment Advisers Act of 1940 §§ 203(l), 203(m); September 2024 SEC Division of Investment Management Update

fact_pattern:
Meridian Capital Advisors LLC ('Meridian') is a registered investment adviser that serves exclusively as the adviser to three institutional private equity fund clients, with aggregate AUM of approximately $4.2 billion. In January 2023, the SEC's Division of Examinations issued a deficiency letter to Meridian following a routine examination. The deficiency letter cited several concerns: (1) Meridian had allocated co-investment opportunities disproportionately to Fund II, whose limited partners included several Meridian principals, without adequate disclosure; (2) Meridian had shifted certain broken-deal expenses from Fund III to Fund I without obtaining consent from Fund I's advisory committee; and (3) Meridian had failed to conduct a reasonable investigation into the valuation methodology used by a third-party appraiser for a $340 million portfolio company acquisition in Fund II.

Meridian's General Counsel, Sandra Whitfield, responded to the deficiency letter by arguing that the SEC's 2019 Fiduciary Interpretation was primarily directed at retail investor relationships and that, as an adviser exclusively to sophisticated institutional fund clients with negotiated limited partnership agreements, Meridian's obligations were governed by the contractual terms of those LPAs rather than by the SEC's articulation of the duty of care. Whitfield further argued that the duty of care as described in the Fiduciary Interpretation was merely a restatement of existing law and created no new obligations, and that the SEC had historically enforced adviser obligations to institutional clients primarily through disclosure-based theories under Sections 206(1) and 206(2) of the Advisers Act, not through a standalone duty of care.

The SEC Enforcement Division subsequently opened a formal investigation into Meridian. In its Wells Notice, the Division cited the 2019 Fiduciary Interpretation as the basis for a duty of care that encompasses an obligation to conduct a 'reasonable investigation' into investments made on behalf of fund clients, and further asserted that this duty applies to private fund advisers regardless of the sophistication of their investor base. Meridian's outside counsel, the firm of Hargrove & Stein LLP, prepared a Wells submission arguing that the SEC was improperly applying a standard developed for retail advisory relationships to an institutional context, and that the Fiduciary Interpretation itself acknowledged that the scope of an adviser's duty depends on the nature of the advisory relationship and the sophistication of the client.

The matter is now before the Commission for a decision on whether to institute an administrative proceeding. The key legal question is whether the SEC's 2019 Fiduciary Interpretation and subsequent agency statements support the application of the duty of care — including the reasonable investigation component — to an investment adviser whose only clients are institutional private fund vehicles.
question: Based on the SEC's own characterization of the 2019 Fiduciary Interpretation and subsequent agency statements as described in the article by Bartels and Kelly, does the SEC's articulated duty of care under Section 206 of the Advisers Act apply to advisers serving exclusively institutional private fund clients? Specifically, what evidence do the authors identify from post-2019 SEC enforcement actions, deficiency letters, and the SEC's private fund adviser rulemaking proposal that addresses whether the duty of care extends beyond retail relationships, and how does this undercut Meridian's defense?
correct_answer:
According to the article by Bartels and Kelly, Meridian's defense that the duty of care applies only to retail advisory relationships is directly contradicted by both the text of the 2019 Fiduciary Interpretation and subsequent SEC statements. The authors specifically note that 'although contemporaneous rulemakings focused on retail investors, the Fiduciary Interpretation addresses an adviser's duties as they relate to both institutional and retail clients.' This is a critical distinction: while Regulation Best Interest was retail-focused, the Fiduciary Interpretation was explicitly broader in scope.

Moreover, the authors identify three specific categories of post-2019 SEC activity that demonstrate the agency's application of the duty of care to institutional and private fund contexts: (1) the SEC has 'referenced the duty of care in enforcement actions... concerning advisers to institutional fund clients,' (2) the SEC has referenced it in 'deficiency letters concerning advisers to institutional fund clients,' and (3) in the SEC's proposal to expand regulation of private fund advisers, the SEC explicitly stated that '[a]dvisers have a fiduciary duty to clients, including private fund clients, that is comprised of a duty of care and a duty of loyalty enforceable under the antifraud provisions of Section 206.' This tripartite evidentiary basis makes clear that the SEC views the duty of care — including its reasonable investigation component — as fully applicable to private fund advisers serving institutional clients.

The authors further note that the Fiduciary Interpretation's characterization as a 'mere compendium' of existing law 'underplays its significance,' because it featured 'the SEC's first extended articulation of a duty of care under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940.' This suggests that even if the duty of care is framed as a restatement, it represents a substantive expansion of the SEC's enforcement toolkit — one that the SEC has already begun deploying against advisers to institutional clients, directly undermining Meridian's contractual-primacy defense.
why_adversarial: This question requires specific knowledge of what Bartels and Kelly identified in their article: that the SEC has already referenced the duty of care in enforcement actions and deficiency letters specifically concerning advisers to institutional fund clients, and that the SEC's private fund adviser rulemaking proposal contained an explicit statement applying the duty of care to private fund clients. A general LLM would know the broad contours of the 2019 Fiduciary Interpretation and Reg BI but would likely not know: (1) that the article specifically distinguishes the Fiduciary Interpretation's scope from Reg BI's retail focus; (2) that the authors document the SEC's post-2019 use of the duty of care in institutional/private fund enforcement contexts; or (3) the specific quotation from the private fund adviser proposal that explicitly names private fund clients as owing a duty of care. Without this document-specific knowledge, a model would likely default to the common but incorrect answer that the duty of care's scope is modulated by client sophistication.
common_wrong_answer: A general LLM would likely argue that while the Fiduciary Interpretation technically applies to all advisory relationships, the scope of the duty of care is significantly attenuated for institutional clients, and that the SEC has historically confined its duty-of-care enforcement to retail contexts. The model would probably cite the general principle that an adviser's obligations may be shaped by the sophistication of the client and the nature of the relationship, and would likely conclude that Meridian has a strong argument that its LPA-governed relationships with sophisticated institutional fund clients reduce or eliminate the independent duty of care. The model would miss the article's specific evidence that the SEC has already applied the duty of care to institutional fund advisers through enforcement actions, deficiency letters, and the private fund adviser rulemaking proposal.
applicable_standard: Section 206(1) and 206(2) of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940; SEC 2019 Fiduciary Interpretation (IA-5248); SEC Proposed Rule on Private Fund Advisers (IA-5955); Regulation Best Interest Rule 15l-1 under Exchange Act §15(l)

fact_pattern:
Marcus Delgado is a registered representative affiliated with Cambridge Investment Research, Inc. (Cambridge) and has been serving retail clients in commission-based brokerage accounts since 2015. In March 2020, one of his longstanding clients, Patricia Nolan, had an existing commission-based brokerage account that had been opened in 2017. Patricia made no new deposits or purchases during the first half of 2020. On June 15, 2020 — approximately two weeks before the Reg BI compliance date — Marcus recommended that Patricia sell her position in a high-yield bond fund and use the proceeds to purchase a variable annuity within the same existing account. Marcus provided Patricia with a detailed suitability analysis and ensured the transaction was suitable under FINRA Rule 2111.

On August 3, 2020, Patricia called Marcus again and asked him to deposit $50,000 of new funds from an inheritance into the same existing account and to recommend an allocation for those funds. Marcus recommended purchasing shares of a proprietary mutual fund that carried a front-end load. Marcus did not deliver any Reg BI disclosure documents or complete a Best Interest Analysis Form at the time of the August transaction, reasoning that Patricia's account had been opened years before July 2020 and that he had already satisfied suitability obligations for this longstanding client.

In November 2020, Cambridge's compliance department conducted a review of Marcus's accounts and flagged the August 2020 transaction. Marcus argued that because Patricia's account predated Reg BI's effective date, neither Reg BI disclosures nor the Best Interest Analysis documentation were required for the August deposit and recommendation. He pointed out that the June 2020 transaction — which was nearly identical in nature — required no Reg BI compliance steps because it predated the regulation's compliance date.

Cambridge's compliance officer, Linda Chen, disagreed with Marcus's position, citing Cambridge's internal procedures derived from the firm's interpretation of the Reg BI FAQ guidance. She noted that the firm's documentation triggers for existing pre-July 2020 accounts were specifically enumerated and that the August transaction triggered at least two separate documentation and disclosure requirements regardless of when the account was originally opened.

Marcus has now escalated the dispute internally, contending that imposing Reg BI obligations on activity in accounts that predate the regulation creates an impermissible retroactive application of the rule. He further argues that since the account terms and conditions were established under the pre-Reg BI suitability standard, those terms should govern all subsequent activity in the account.
question: Under Cambridge's Reg BI FAQ procedures for accounts existing prior to the initial July 2020 delivery date, what specific transactional events in Marcus's August 2020 activity independently triggered both (a) Reg BI disclosure obligations and (b) Best Interest Analysis documentation requirements, and why does Marcus's argument that pre-July 2020 accounts are grandfathered from Reg BI requirements fail based on the document's enumerated trigger events?
correct_answer:
According to Cambridge's Reg BI FAQ document, Marcus's August 2020 activity triggered obligations under two distinct categories. First, for Reg BI Disclosures on accounts existing prior to the initial delivery date of July 2020, the document specifically enumerates 'Deposit/transfer in of new funds or securities' and 'Buy/Sell/Hold recommendations for commission accounts' as independent trigger events. Patricia's $50,000 deposit of inherited funds constituted a 'deposit/transfer in of new funds,' and Marcus's subsequent recommendation to purchase a proprietary front-load mutual fund constituted a 'Buy/Sell/Hold recommendation for commission accounts.' Both independently required Reg BI disclosure delivery.

Second, for Best Interest Analysis documentation, the document separately enumerates triggers for new accounts including 'Deposit/transfer in of new funds/securities' and 'Buy/sell/hold recommendation.' While the Best Interest Analysis triggers are listed under 'New accounts,' the deposit of new funds and the buy recommendation each independently triggered documentation requirements. The document makes clear that even for pre-existing accounts, the enumerated transactional events — not the account opening date — are what trigger compliance obligations post-July 2020.

Marcus's grandfathering argument fails because the Cambridge FAQ explicitly contemplates that accounts existing prior to July 2020 have their own specific disclosure trigger framework. The regulation and Cambridge's implementing procedures are transaction-triggered, not account-triggered. The fact that Reg BI disclosures for pre-July 2020 accounts were 'Delivered through the terms and conditions of the Client Information and Suitability Form for new accounts after July' does not exempt subsequent qualifying transactions from triggering fresh disclosure and documentation obligations. Each enumerated event — new fund deposits and buy/sell/hold recommendations — creates an independent obligation regardless of account vintage.
why_adversarial: This question requires knowing the specific enumerated trigger events listed in the Cambridge Reg BI FAQ document for (1) Reg BI Disclosures for accounts existing prior to July 2020 and (2) Best Interest Analysis documentation. The document distinguishes between these two categories and lists slightly different trigger events for each. A general LLM would know that Reg BI became effective June 30, 2020, and would understand the general care and disclosure obligations, but would not know that Cambridge's specific FAQ enumerates 'Deposit/transfer in of new funds or securities' and 'Buy/Sell/Hold recommendations for commission accounts' as separate triggers for pre-existing accounts, nor that the Best Interest Analysis has its own parallel but distinct trigger list. The temporal trap is that the June 2020 transaction genuinely did not require Reg BI compliance (pre-compliance date), but the nearly identical August 2020 activity in the same pre-existing account did — based on specific enumerated triggers that a general model would not know to cite.
common_wrong_answer: A general LLM would likely focus on the broad principle that Reg BI applied to all recommendations after June 30, 2020, and would correctly identify that the August transaction required Reg BI compliance. However, it would likely state that the obligation was triggered simply because the recommendation occurred after the compliance date, without identifying the specific enumerated trigger events (deposit/transfer of new funds AND buy/sell/hold recommendation) as independent triggers, and without distinguishing between the separate Reg BI Disclosure triggers for pre-existing accounts versus the Best Interest Analysis triggers. The model would also likely miss that Cambridge's FAQ creates a distinct disclosure delivery mechanism for pre-July 2020 accounts through the 'terms and conditions of the Client Information and Suitability Form' and would not accurately describe how the two parallel trigger frameworks operate differently for pre-existing versus new accounts.
applicable_standard: Reg BI Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(ii) (Care Obligation); Reg BI Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(iii) (Conflict of Interest Obligation); Exchange Act §15(l); Cambridge Investment Research Reg BI FAQ internal procedures for Form CRS, Reg BI Disclosures, and Best Interest Analysis documentation triggers; FINRA Rule 2111 (pre-Reg BI suitability standard)

fact_pattern:
Heartland National Bank, N.A. (assets: $14.2 billion) launched 'SmartPath Invest,' an AI-driven robo-advisory platform in January 2025, offering retail nondeposit investment products (RNDIPs) through its consumer banking website. The platform uses a proprietary machine learning algorithm trained on customer deposit data, transaction history, and self-reported risk tolerance questionnaires to generate automated portfolio recommendations consisting of mutual funds, ETFs, and variable annuities. SmartPath Invest is operated through a third-party arrangement with FinEdge Technologies, LLC, a registered broker-dealer, under a networking agreement structured to comply with Regulation R's bank networking exceptions.

In February 2025, the OCC's Large Bank Supervision team initiated an examination of Heartland's RNDIP program. During the examination, examiners discovered that SmartPath Invest's AI algorithm occasionally recommended variable annuity products to customers who had logged into the bank's online deposit platform—presenting the recommendations in a manner that appeared alongside FDIC-insured deposit account information. The disclosures stating that products were 'Not FDIC Insured,' 'Not a Deposit,' 'Not Guaranteed by the Bank,' and 'May Lose Value' were present but rendered in a smaller font below the fold of the webpage, requiring users to scroll. The AI-generated recommendations did not include any human review before being presented to customers.

Heartland's Chief Risk Officer, Diana Vasquez, argued during the examination that the bank had conducted thorough model risk management validation of the AI algorithm under OCC Bulletin 2011-12 (SR 11-7), and that the algorithm's recommendation engine was simply a 'tool' analogous to providing investment literature, not constituting a 'recommendation' under Regulation Best Interest. She further contended that because OCC Bulletin 2025-4, issued March 20, 2025, removed all references to reputation risk from OCC examination guidance, the examiners could no longer cite reputational concerns as a basis for supervisory criticism of how SmartPath Invest presented products alongside deposit information.

The OCC examiners also noted that Heartland had not updated its Program Management Statement since 2019, before the launch of SmartPath Invest, and that the bank's board of directors had not formally reviewed or approved the AI-driven RNDIP delivery channel. The third-party arrangement with FinEdge was governed by a service-level agreement but Heartland had not conducted an independent due diligence review of FinEdge's compliance with the Interagency Statement on Retail Sales of Nondeposit Investment Products since 2021.

In April 2025, three retail customers filed complaints alleging they believed the variable annuity products recommended by SmartPath Invest were FDIC-insured deposit products, citing the seamless integration of the recommendations into the bank's online deposit interface.
question: Under the June 2024 version of the OCC's Comptroller's Handbook on Retail Nondeposit Investment Products—as modified by OCC Bulletin 2025-4 and OCC Bulletin 2025-25—is Diana Vasquez correct that the OCC examiners can no longer use reputation risk as a basis for supervisory criticism of SmartPath Invest's presentation of RNDIPs alongside deposit products? Additionally, what specific risk categories from the Handbook's risk assessment framework REMAIN available to examiners to address the customer confusion issues, and how does the Handbook's treatment of RNDIP delivery channels and the Interagency Statement requirements apply to AI-driven recommendation platforms that were not contemplated when the original guidance was issued?
correct_answer:
Diana Vasquez is partially correct but substantially wrong in her broader conclusion. OCC Bulletin 2025-4 did remove references to reputation risk from the Comptroller's Handbook, including the Retail Nondeposit Investment Products booklet (Version 2.0, June 2024), as confirmed by the strikethrough notation in the booklet itself. However, the removal of reputation risk as an examination category does NOT eliminate the OCC's ability to cite supervisory concerns about Heartland's RNDIP program. The Handbook explicitly identifies four other risk categories that remain fully applicable: compliance risk, operational risk, strategic risk, and credit risk. The customer confusion scenario described—where variable annuities are presented alongside FDIC-insured deposit information with inadequate disclosures—would be examined primarily under compliance risk (failure to comply with the Interagency Statement on Retail Sales of Nondeposit Investment Products, which requires prominent disclosures that products are not FDIC insured, not deposits, not guaranteed by the bank, and may lose value) and operational risk (inadequate controls over the AI-driven delivery channel, failure to ensure disclosures are presented conspicuously, and deficient third-party risk management of the FinEdge relationship).

The Handbook's section on RNDIP Delivery Channels and the Interagency Statement requirements apply regardless of whether the delivery mechanism is a human sales representative or an automated AI platform. The Handbook requires that the bank's Program Management Statement and policies and procedures be updated to address all delivery channels through which RNDIPs are offered. Heartland's failure to update its Program Management Statement since 2019—before SmartPath Invest was launched—and the board's failure to formally approve the AI-driven channel constitute independent supervisory deficiencies under the Handbook's risk management framework, specifically under the 'Adoption of Program Management Statement and Policies and Procedures' and 'Program Management' sections. The Handbook requires board-level oversight and approval of RNDIP program parameters.

Further, OCC Bulletin 2025-25, which limits the OCC's use of expanded examination procedures for community banks, does not apply to Heartland ($14.2 billion in assets), meaning the full expanded examination procedures in the RNDIP booklet remain available to examiners. The novel question of whether an AI algorithm's output constitutes a 'recommendation' under Regulation Best Interest is separate from the OCC's supervisory authority over how the bank presents RNDIPs; the OCC's concern is with the bank's compliance with banking laws, the Interagency Statement, and safe-and-sound banking practices, not solely with securities law definitions of 'recommendation.' The Interagency Statement's disclosure requirements apply to all retail sales of nondeposit investment products regardless of how the recommendation is generated.
why_adversarial: This question requires specific knowledge of three document-level details that a general LLM would not know: (1) OCC Bulletin 2025-4's removal of reputation risk from the Handbook as of March 20, 2025, evidenced by strikethrough notation in the document; (2) the exact remaining risk categories enumerated in the RNDIP booklet (compliance, operational, strategic, credit); and (3) OCC Bulletin 2025-25's limitation applying only to community banks, not to a $14.2 billion bank. A general model would likely either not know about the reputation risk removal at all, or would incorrectly assume the removal eliminates the OCC's ability to address the customer confusion issues. The question also tests whether the model knows the Handbook's specific structural requirements for Program Management Statements and board approval, and how the Interagency Statement's disclosure requirements operate independently of Reg BI's 'recommendation' definition.
common_wrong_answer: A general LLM would likely respond in one of two incorrect ways: (1) It would not be aware of OCC Bulletin 2025-4's removal of reputation risk and would instead argue that reputation risk IS available as a basis for supervisory criticism, citing general principles about banks needing to protect their reputation; or (2) it might correctly identify the reputation risk removal but then incorrectly conclude that the OCC's supervisory tools are significantly diminished, failing to identify the specific remaining risk categories (compliance, operational, strategic, credit) enumerated in the Handbook. Most models would also fail to correctly apply OCC Bulletin 2025-25's community bank limitation, potentially arguing it restricts examination of Heartland when it does not apply to a bank of that size. Additionally, a general model would likely conflate the OCC's supervisory authority over RNDIP disclosure practices with the SEC's Reg BI framework, incorrectly analyzing the issue primarily through a securities law lens rather than through the OCC's banking safety-and-soundness and Interagency Statement framework.
applicable_standard: OCC Comptroller's Handbook, Retail Nondeposit Investment Products (Version 2.0, June 2024); OCC Bulletin 2025-4 (removal of reputation risk references, March 20, 2025); OCC Bulletin 2025-25 (community bank examination limitations); Interagency Statement on Retail Sales of Nondeposit Investment Products; 12 CFR Part 9 (Fiduciary Activities of National Banks); OCC Bulletin 2011-12 (Model Risk Management); Regulation R (17 CFR Part 247); Regulation Best Interest (17 CFR § 240.15l-1)

fact_pattern:
Heartland National Bank, N.A. ('Heartland'), a nationally chartered bank, operates a trust department that administers $4.2 billion in collective investment funds (CIFs) under 12 CFR 9.18. In January 2022, Heartland established the 'Heartland Strategic Equity CIF,' a fund available exclusively to its fiduciary accounts, including approximately 340 ERISA-governed pension plans and 120 non-ERISA personal trust accounts. Heartland delegated day-to-day portfolio management of the CIF to Ridgeline Capital Advisors LLC ('Ridgeline'), an SEC-registered investment adviser under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940, pursuant to a written sub-advisory agreement. Ridgeline was selected after a competitive search process documented by the trust committee.

The CIF's written plan, maintained per 12 CFR 9.18(b), stated that the fund would invest in large-cap U.S. equities with a value orientation and that no more than 5% of fund assets could be invested in any single issuer. The plan also specified that Heartland's trust department retained responsibility for fund valuation, admissions and withdrawals of participating accounts, and compliance with the fund's written plan. Ridgeline's sub-advisory agreement gave it discretion over individual security selection within the parameters of the written plan.

Between March and August 2022, Ridgeline gradually concentrated 14.2% of the CIF's assets in a single technology company, TechNova Inc., which was neither a large-cap stock nor a value-oriented holding. TechNova subsequently lost 68% of its value in September 2022, causing the CIF to decline 19.3% in a single quarter. Heartland's internal audit function had not reviewed the CIF's portfolio holdings during this period, and the trust committee had not received any exception reports flagging the concentration breach.

Meanwhile, PlanServ Administrators Inc. ('PlanServ'), a third-party administrator for 78 of the ERISA plans invested in the CIF, had recommended participation in the Heartland Strategic Equity CIF to its plan sponsor clients based on the fund's stated investment parameters. PlanServ is not a registered investment adviser and disclaimed fiduciary status in its service agreements with the plan sponsors.

The Department of Labor opens an investigation. The OCC separately initiates a supervisory review. Several plan sponsors and individual trust beneficiaries file suit. The ERISA plan sponsors argue that Heartland, Ridgeline, and PlanServ each bear liability. Individual trust beneficiaries argue that Heartland's failure to monitor the sub-adviser and the CIF's compliance with its own written plan constitutes a breach of fiduciary duty under both 12 CFR Part 9 and applicable state trust law.
question: Under the OCC's Comptroller's Handbook guidance on Collective Investment Funds and 12 CFR 9.18, what specific ongoing administrative and supervisory obligations did Heartland retain as the administering bank that could NOT be delegated to Ridgeline regardless of the sub-advisory agreement, and how does the Handbook's framework for board and management supervision, fund administration, and audit/compliance monitoring create a liability allocation between Heartland and Ridgeline that differs from what would apply if Ridgeline were simply an IA sub-adviser to a registered investment company under the Investment Company Act of 1940? Additionally, under the Handbook's risk management framework, which specific category of risk — compliance, operational, strategic, or reputation — does the failure to monitor adherence to the CIF's written plan primarily implicate, and what does the Handbook require of the bank's internal controls to mitigate that risk?
correct_answer:
Under 12 CFR 9.18(b) and the OCC Comptroller's Handbook on CIFs, Heartland as the administering national bank retains non-delegable responsibility for maintaining and enforcing the fund's written plan, including ensuring that all investments comply with the plan's stated parameters (here, the large-cap value mandate and the 5% single-issuer concentration limit). The Handbook specifically requires that the bank's board or trust committee exercise ongoing supervision over fund administration, that policies and procedures ensure compliance with the written plan, and that admissions, withdrawals, and valuations are conducted by the bank — not the sub-adviser. Even where day-to-day portfolio management is delegated, 12 CFR 9.18 places the ultimate fiduciary and administrative obligation on the administering bank, which must maintain audit and compliance monitoring systems capable of detecting deviations from the written plan. The Handbook's section on fund administration makes clear that the bank must conduct or oversee regular portfolio reviews to verify plan compliance — a duty that cannot be contractually shifted to the sub-adviser.

This differs fundamentally from the Investment Company Act of 1940 framework, where a registered investment company's board of directors has oversight responsibility under Sections 15 and 36, and the investment adviser and sub-adviser relationship is governed by separate contractual and statutory duties. Under the '40 Act, a sub-adviser's deviation from its mandate creates primary liability for the sub-adviser under its advisory agreement and potentially under Section 36(b) for breach of fiduciary duty with respect to compensation, but the fund's board has an independent duty of oversight that is qualitatively different from the bank's non-delegable administrative duties under 9.18. The Handbook's Appendix C specifically addresses the distinction between CIFs and '40 Act funds, noting that CIFs are excluded from registration under the Investment Company Act precisely because bank fiduciary regulation provides a parallel — but structurally different — supervisory framework. Under 9.18, there is no independent board of directors; the bank itself is the fiduciary, and its trust committee functions as the oversight body with direct, non-delegable liability.

The Handbook's risk management framework identifies the failure to monitor adherence to the CIF's written plan as primarily a compliance risk — defined in the Handbook as the risk of legal or regulatory sanctions, financial loss, or damage to reputation arising from failure to comply with laws, regulations, rules, internal policies, or the fund's own governing documents. The Handbook requires that the bank maintain management information systems and exception reporting mechanisms sufficient to flag breaches of the written plan's investment parameters, and that the internal audit function independently verify compliance at regular intervals. Heartland's failure to generate exception reports flagging the 14.2% concentration in TechNova and the trust committee's failure to receive such reports represent a breakdown in precisely the compliance risk controls the Handbook mandates, making Heartland primarily liable under the OCC framework regardless of Ridgeline's concurrent breach of its sub-advisory mandate.
why_adversarial: This question requires specific knowledge of the OCC Comptroller's Handbook on CIFs' structure — particularly its delineation of non-delegable bank duties under 12 CFR 9.18(b), the specific risk categories (compliance, operational, strategic, reputation) defined in the Handbook, and the Handbook's explicit comparison of CIFs to '40 Act funds in Appendix C. A general LLM would likely apply generic fiduciary delegation principles or conflate the bank's duties with those of a mutual fund board, missing the OCC-specific framework that makes the administering bank's liability qualitatively different and non-delegable. The Handbook's specific organizational structure — Board and Management Supervision, Policies and Procedures, Fund Administration, Audit and Compliance Monitoring, and Management Information Systems — creates a framework that a model relying on general securities law knowledge would not accurately reconstruct.
common_wrong_answer: A general LLM would likely answer that Heartland and Ridgeline share liability in proportion to their respective roles, analogizing to the mutual fund sub-adviser framework where the sub-adviser bears primary liability for portfolio management decisions and the fund board has a secondary oversight duty. The model would likely classify the risk as 'operational risk' rather than 'compliance risk,' conflate the bank's duties with those of a '40 Act fund board, and suggest that the sub-advisory agreement could effectively shift primary liability to Ridgeline for the concentration breach. It would also likely miss the Handbook's specific requirement for exception reporting and management information systems as part of the bank's non-delegable compliance infrastructure, and would not reference 12 CFR 9.18(b)'s written plan requirement or Appendix C's explicit CIF/'40 Act comparison.
applicable_standard: 12 CFR 9.18 (Collective Investment Funds); 12 CFR 9.18(b) (Administrative Requirements including written plan); OCC Comptroller's Handbook, 'Collective Investment Funds' (May 2014) — sections on Board and Management Supervision, Fund Administration, Audit and Compliance Monitoring, Management Information Systems, Compliance Risk, Operational Risk; Appendix B (12 CFR 9.18(b) Administrative Requirements); Appendix C (CIFs and the '40 Act); Investment Company Act of 1940 Sections 3(c)(3), 3(c)(11), 15, 36; ERISA Sections 3(21), 405(a)

fact_pattern:
Meridian National Bank, a nationally chartered commercial bank headquartered in Charlotte, North Carolina, has operated a traditional trust and custody division under 12 CFR Part 9 since 1998, holding equities, fixed-income securities, and physical precious metals on behalf of institutional and high-net-worth clients. In March 2021, Meridian's board of directors approved a strategic initiative to expand its custody services to include digital assets, specifically Bitcoin and Ethereum, for existing fiduciary clients whose investment policy statements were amended to permit up to 5% allocation to cryptocurrency.

Meridian's Chief Risk Officer, Sandra Holt, engaged outside counsel to determine whether the bank needed to obtain a new or separate charter, special purpose trust license, or specific OCC approval before offering cryptocurrency custody. The bank's compliance team drafted a memo concluding that because Meridian already held a trust powers authorization under 12 CFR 9.2 and routinely custodied intangible assets, no additional regulatory permission was needed beyond updating internal policies and risk controls. The memo cited general OCC guidance on fiduciary activities from the Comptroller's Handbook.

However, Meridian's competitor, Pinnacle National Bank, took a different approach. Pinnacle's legal team argued that cryptocurrency custody—specifically the holding of unique cryptographic keys on behalf of customers—constituted an entirely novel activity that fell outside traditional banking powers, and that explicit OCC interpretive guidance was required before proceeding. Pinnacle delayed its cryptocurrency custody launch by nine months while seeking external legal opinions.

Meanwhile, Meridian launched its cryptocurrency custody service in June 2021, holding private cryptographic keys in a combination of hardware security modules (HSMs) and multi-signature cold storage wallets. By December 2021, Meridian custodied approximately $340 million in Bitcoin and $85 million in Ethereum across 127 fiduciary accounts. During a routine OCC examination in Q1 2022, the examiner raised questions about the legal basis for Meridian's cryptocurrency custody activities and whether the bank had properly established its authority to engage in this specific activity.

Additionally, Meridian's trust division had begun providing cryptocurrency custody not only in its capacity as a fiduciary under 12 CFR Part 9, but also in a non-fiduciary custodial capacity for several corporate treasury clients who simply wanted secure key storage without any investment discretion or advisory relationship. The OCC examiner specifically questioned whether the bank's authority to hold cryptographic keys extended to both fiduciary and non-fiduciary custody capacities, and under what specific legal authority the non-fiduciary custody of cryptographic keys was permissible.
question: Under OCC Interpretive Letter #1170 (July 2020), what is the specific legal basis cited for a national bank's authority to provide cryptocurrency custody services by holding unique cryptographic keys, and does this authority apply only to fiduciary custody under 12 CFR Part 9, or does it also encompass non-fiduciary custodial services? Additionally, does the letter require national banks to obtain separate OCC approval before offering cryptocurrency custody, or is this activity treated as a permissible banking service available to any national bank that effectively manages risks and complies with applicable law?
correct_answer:
OCC Interpretive Letter #1170, issued July 22, 2020, concludes that a national bank may provide cryptocurrency custody services for customers, including by holding the unique cryptographic keys associated with cryptocurrency. The letter does not limit this authority to fiduciary custody under 12 CFR Part 9; rather, it addresses custody broadly as a permissible banking service. The letter frames cryptocurrency custody as a modern form of traditional bank custody activities, analogous to how banks have historically safeguarded assets on behalf of customers in both fiduciary and non-fiduciary capacities.

Critically, the letter does not require banks to obtain separate or special OCC approval before offering cryptocurrency custody. Instead, it reaffirms the OCC's position that national banks may provide permissible banking services to any lawful business they choose, including cryptocurrency businesses, 'so long as they effectively manage the risks and comply with applicable law.' The operative standard is risk management adequacy and legal compliance, not prior regulatory approval for the activity itself. The letter also explicitly extends this conclusion to Federal savings associations (FSAs).

Therefore, Meridian National Bank's approach—launching cryptocurrency custody services based on existing authority while implementing appropriate risk controls—is more consistent with the framework established by IL #1170 than Pinnacle's approach of seeking separate external confirmation. The OCC examiner's inquiry would be properly focused not on whether Meridian had legal authority (which IL #1170 confirms it did), but on whether Meridian had implemented controls commensurate with the risks of holding cryptographic keys, including cybersecurity, key management, and BSA/AML compliance. Both fiduciary and non-fiduciary custody of cryptographic keys fall within the scope of the letter's authorization.
why_adversarial: This question requires specific knowledge of OCC Interpretive Letter #1170's actual conclusions and scope. A general LLM would likely assume that cryptocurrency custody is a novel, high-risk activity requiring special regulatory approval or licensing, or that it falls exclusively under fiduciary powers (12 CFR Part 9). The letter's key holding—that crypto custody is simply a modern extension of traditional custodial banking powers available without special approval—is counterintuitive and specific to this document. The letter's explicit extension to FSAs, its framing as a permissible banking service rather than a new power, and its emphasis on risk management rather than prior approval are all details that cannot be derived from general legal knowledge. Most LLMs would incorrectly suggest the bank needed separate OCC approval or would conflate this with the 12 CFR Part 9 fiduciary framework exclusively.
common_wrong_answer: A general LLM would likely answer that cryptocurrency custody is a novel banking activity requiring either (a) specific OCC approval or a no-objection letter before commencement, (b) trust powers authorization under 12 CFR Part 9 limiting the activity to fiduciary accounts only, or (c) a special purpose national bank charter. The LLM might also incorrectly state that IL #1170 only addresses fiduciary custody of digital assets or that it imposes specific pre-conditions beyond general risk management. Many models would conflate this with the OCC's separate conditional chartering framework for fintech companies or suggest that the bank would need to apply for expanded powers under 12 CFR 5.20.
applicable_standard: OCC Interpretive Letter #1170 (July 22, 2020); 12 CFR Part 9 (Fiduciary Activities of National Banks); OCC Comptroller's Handbook on Fiduciary Activities; Joint Statement on Risk-Focused BSA/AML Supervision (July 22, 2019); 12 USC 24 (Seventh) (incidental powers of national banks)

fact_pattern:
In March 2002, Heritage Federal Savings Association, a federally chartered thrift institution headquartered in Springfield, Illinois, established a trust department and began administering fiduciary accounts. By September 2002, the trust department managed approximately $180 million in assets across 340 individual trust accounts and 45 tax-qualified retirement plan accounts. Heritage's trust committee, chaired by Senior Vice President Margaret Dunlap, proposed creating two collective investment funds: (1) the Heritage Balanced Growth Fund, a common trust fund for individual fiduciary accounts held as trustee, executor, administrator, and guardian, and (2) the Heritage Retirement Equity Fund, a collective investment fund for the tax-qualified retirement plan accounts.

Heritage's outside counsel, the law firm of Whitmore & Strauss LLP, advised Dunlap that because Heritage was a savings association — not a national bank — it could not simply launch collective investment funds without registering them as investment companies with the Securities and Exchange Commission under the Investment Company Act of 1940. Counsel specifically noted that the SEC registration exemption in Section 3(c)(3) of the Investment Company Act historically applied only to banks, and that savings associations were not included in the statutory definition of 'bank' for purposes of that exemption. Whitmore & Strauss recommended Heritage either register the funds with the SEC at significant compliance cost (estimated at $450,000 in initial legal and filing fees, plus $175,000 annually in ongoing reporting obligations) or abandon the collective fund initiative entirely.

Dunlap was frustrated by this advice and sought a second opinion from a former OCC examiner, Charles Redding, who had recently entered private consulting. Redding reviewed the relevant statutes and told Dunlap that Whitmore & Strauss's advice was outdated and incorrect, and that Heritage could offer both funds without SEC registration. Dunlap, uncertain whom to believe, escalated the matter to Heritage's board of directors, which tabled the proposal pending regulatory clarification.

The board's concern was primarily practical: if Heritage offered the funds without SEC registration and the counsel's original advice was correct, the association could face SEC enforcement action, potential rescission obligations to all participating accounts, and reputational damage. On the other hand, if Redding was correct, Heritage was foregoing a significant competitive advantage and cost savings for its trust customers — the very customers who would benefit from automatic diversification, reduced fees, and favorable investment performance that collective funds typically provide.

The trust department estimated that launching the two funds would reduce per-account investment management fees by approximately 35 basis points and improve portfolio diversification for smaller trust accounts that individually held fewer than 15 securities. The retirement plan accounts, which were tax-exempt, would particularly benefit because the pass-through of capital gains and losses — typically a disadvantage for taxable participants — would have no adverse tax consequence for them.
question: Under the regulatory framework applicable to Heritage Federal Savings Association as of 2002, was Whitmore & Strauss LLP's advice correct that Heritage must register its proposed collective investment funds with the SEC, or was consultant Redding correct that no SEC registration was required? Identify the specific statutory provision that resolved this issue for savings associations, explain when it became effective, and describe what prior legal barrier it eliminated.
correct_answer:
Consultant Redding was correct, and Whitmore & Strauss LLP's advice was outdated. Section 223 of the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act (GLBA), enacted on November 12, 1999, amended Section 2(a)(5) of the Investment Company Act of 1940 in a way that permitted savings associations to offer common and collective funds to their trust customers without registering those funds with the SEC. Prior to the GLBA, savings associations were excluded from the definition of 'bank' under the Investment Company Act, which meant the Section 3(c)(3) exemption from registration — available to bank-maintained common trust funds and collective investment funds — did not extend to savings associations. The GLBA's amendment resolved this disparity.

As the OTS Trust and Asset Management Handbook (Section 880) explicitly states: 'Savings associations will be permitted for the first time to offer common and collective funds to its trust customers without having to register them with the Securities and Exchange Commission. This result was achieved by the language in Section 223 of the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act that amended Section 2(a)(5) of the Investment Company Act of 1940.' This was a counterintuitive development because, for decades, the conventional understanding was that savings associations lacked this exemption and were required to register collective funds as investment companies — a costly and burdensome process that effectively prevented most thrifts from offering such products.

Additionally, OTS Regulation §550.260(a) authorized savings associations to invest fiduciary funds in collective investment funds established and administered in accordance with the OCC's 12 CFR §9.18. Heritage would need to comply with §9.18's requirements — including establishing a written plan approved by the board of directors (or a designated committee), with provisions covering investment powers, fee allocation, admission/withdrawal terms, valuation methods, and audit procedures — but SEC registration was not required. Heritage's board should have proceeded with the collective fund initiative subject to §9.18 compliance, and Whitmore & Strauss's advice reflected the pre-GLBA legal landscape that was no longer applicable.
why_adversarial: This question is adversarial because a general LLM would likely know that the Investment Company Act's Section 3(c)(3) exemption applies to banks but would not necessarily know that savings associations were historically excluded from that exemption and that Section 223 of the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act specifically resolved this issue by amending Section 2(a)(5) of the Investment Company Act. The OTS Handbook's explicit statement that savings associations were 'permitted for the first time' to offer collective funds without SEC registration is a specific, counterintuitive fact buried in this guidance document. A model relying on general knowledge might assume that all depository institutions, including savings associations, always had this exemption, or conversely might agree with the outside counsel that registration was still required. The precise mechanism — Section 223 of GLBA amending Section 2(a)(5) — and the specific authorization under OTS Regulation §550.260(a) cross-referencing OCC §9.18 are granular details that require document-level knowledge.
common_wrong_answer: A general LLM would likely respond that savings associations, as federally regulated depository institutions, have always been exempt from SEC registration for collective investment funds under the Investment Company Act, just like national banks — essentially treating all depository institutions identically. Alternatively, a model might agree with Whitmore & Strauss that savings associations still need to register because they are not 'banks' under the Investment Company Act, failing to recognize the GLBA amendment. The model would be unlikely to cite Section 223 of GLBA or the specific amendment to Section 2(a)(5) of the Investment Company Act, and would almost certainly not reference OTS Regulation §550.260(a) or the cross-reference to 12 CFR §9.18.
applicable_standard: Section 223 of the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act (Pub. L. 106-102); Section 2(a)(5) and Section 3(c)(3) of the Investment Company Act of 1940; 12 CFR §9.18 (OCC Collective Investment Fund regulations); OTS Regulation §550.260(a); IRC §584 (common trust fund tax exemption); Revenue Ruling 81-100 (collective investment fund tax exemption); OTS Trust and Asset Management Handbook Section 880

fact_pattern:
Ridgemont National Bank operates a trust department that administers approximately $2.3 billion in fiduciary assets across 4,200 accounts. In March 2024, the bank's Senior Trust Investment Officer, Diana Choi, is reviewing the Hargrove Family Trust, a $14.7 million irrevocable trust established in 1998 under Ohio law. The trust's governing instrument contains a specialized investment clause that expressly authorizes retention of concentrated holdings in Meridian Industries, Inc. (a mid-cap industrial conglomerate), and further states: 'The Trustee shall not sell, exchange, or otherwise dispose of shares of Meridian Industries, Inc. without the prior written consent of the Trust Protector.' The Trust Protector, Harold Vance, is 91 years old, resides in a memory care facility, and has been unresponsive to correspondence for 18 months. No successor Trust Protector is named in the instrument.

Meridian Industries currently constitutes 62% of the trust's portfolio. Over the past year, Meridian's stock has declined 34% due to a failed acquisition, an SEC accounting investigation, and two credit downgrades. The bank's internal equity research team has placed Meridian on its 'Sell' list, and the bank's approved investment policy recommends no single equity position exceed 15% of a fiduciary account's total value. The trust's three income beneficiaries—adult children of the settlor—have written to the bank demanding immediate diversification, arguing the bank is breaching its fiduciary duty by retaining the concentrated position.

Separately, Ridgemont's wealth management division (a separately registered investment adviser under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940) manages a $9 million discretionary advisory account for one of those same beneficiaries, Carolyn Hargrove. Her advisory account also holds a 40% position in Meridian Industries acquired at her prior instruction, but the investment advisory agreement contains no retention clause—only a general statement that the adviser will manage the account 'in the client's best interest consistent with her stated objectives and risk tolerance.' Carolyn's risk profile is 'moderate growth' and her IPS caps single-position concentration at 20%.

Diana Choi must now decide: (1) whether to sell the Meridian concentration in the Hargrove Family Trust, and (2) whether to sell the Meridian concentration in Carolyn's advisory account. The bank's compliance officer, James Redfield, argues that the same prudent investor analysis should apply identically to both accounts, since the same stock is involved and the bank owes fiduciary duties in both contexts.
question: Under the OCC/OTS framework for bank fiduciary activities as set forth in 12 CFR Part 9 and the OTS Trust and Asset Management Handbook (Section 800), what is the PRIMARY constraint that governs the trust department's investment decision regarding the Meridian concentration in the Hargrove Family Trust, and how does this specifically differ from the standard that would apply to Carolyn's advisory account under the Investment Advisers Act? Why is compliance officer Redfield's assertion that the same prudent investor analysis applies identically to both accounts incorrect?
correct_answer:
Under the OTS Trust and Asset Management Handbook Section 800, the PRIMARY investment constraint for bank fiduciary accounts is the governing instrument, not a generalized prudent investor standard. The Handbook explicitly establishes a hierarchy of asset management constraints: first, 'the specific investment requirements outlined in the governing instrument'; second, 'applicable law, that will include state prudent investment statutes'; third, 'generally accepted fiduciary principles'; and finally, 'account objectives and goals.' The Handbook further states that the governing instrument provides the 'primary investment guidance' and warns that 'failure to [pay close attention to the requirements outlined within the governing instrument] can result in a breach of fiduciary duty and subject the savings association to litigation and financial loss.' This means that even where the bank's own investment policy recommends a 15% single-position cap, and even where prudent investor principles would ordinarily require diversification, the specialized retention clause in the Hargrove trust instrument mandating retention of Meridian shares absent Trust Protector consent creates a binding constraint that takes hierarchical priority. The bank may face liability for selling Meridian without complying with the governing instrument's consent requirement, regardless of the stock's poor performance.

By contrast, Carolyn's advisory account is governed by the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 and the fiduciary duty articulated thereunder (as reinforced by SEC v. Capital Gains Research Bureau and Regulation Best Interest for any dual-hatted recommendations). The advisory agreement contains no retention clause—only a best-interest standard. With Meridian at 40% concentration in a moderate-growth account whose IPS caps single positions at 20%, the adviser has both the authority and the affirmative duty to reduce the position to comply with the client's stated risk parameters. There is no governing-instrument primacy doctrine under the Advisers Act; the adviser's fiduciary obligation to act in the client's best interest, informed by the IPS and suitability profile, controls.

Redfield's assertion is therefore specifically wrong because it ignores the OTS Handbook's explicit hierarchical framework in which the governing instrument supersedes general prudent investor principles for trust accounts. The two accounts are governed by fundamentally different regulatory regimes with different primary constraints, even though both involve fiduciary relationships with the same institution.
why_adversarial: This question requires knowledge of the specific hierarchical ordering of asset management constraints as articulated in OTS Trust Handbook Section 800—namely that the governing instrument is the 'primary investment guidance' and takes precedence over state prudent investor statutes, general fiduciary principles, and account objectives. A general-knowledge LLM would likely default to the Uniform Prudent Investor Act's diversification mandate (which most law school curricula and bar prep emphasize) and conclude that the bank must diversify both accounts under the same analysis. The document's explicit statement that governing instrument constraints come first—ahead of prudent investor statutes—and that violation of governing instrument terms independently constitutes breach of fiduciary duty, is the specific knowledge needed to answer correctly. The counterintuitive result is that retaining the concentrated, declining position may actually be the legally required course of action for the trust account.
common_wrong_answer: A general LLM would likely state that under the Uniform Prudent Investor Act and general fiduciary principles, the bank has a duty to diversify both accounts and that retaining a 62% concentrated position in a declining stock is per se imprudent regardless of what the governing instrument says. It would likely argue that modern prudent investor standards override restrictive trust provisions, especially given the magnitude of the decline and the beneficiaries' objections. It would agree with Redfield that the same prudent investor analysis applies to both accounts, perhaps distinguishing only on the degree of concentration. This answer ignores the OTS Handbook's explicit primacy of governing instrument provisions over prudent investor statutes in the constraint hierarchy.
applicable_standard: 12 CFR Part 9 (OCC Fiduciary Activities); OTS Trust and Asset Management Handbook Section 800 (Asset Management Constraints hierarchy: governing instrument → applicable law/state prudent investment statutes → generally accepted fiduciary principles → account objectives); Investment Advisers Act of 1940 §§ 206(1)-(2); SEC v. Capital Gains Research Bureau, 375 U.S. 180 (1963); Uniform Prudent Investor Act § 3 (diversification)

fact_pattern:
Meridian National Bank, a nationally chartered bank headquartered in Dallas, Texas, with $4.2 billion in total assets, has been exploring cryptocurrency-related services since mid-2020. In September 2021, Meridian's board of directors approved a strategic initiative to offer institutional cryptocurrency custody services, allowing qualified institutional clients to store Bitcoin and Ethereum private keys through Meridian's newly developed cold-storage infrastructure. Meridian's Chief Risk Officer, Sandra Velasquez, prepared a comprehensive 47-page risk assessment covering AML/BSA compliance, cybersecurity protocols, insurance coverage, and operational resilience. The bank also hired a team of six blockchain engineers and two digital asset compliance specialists.

On October 15, 2021, Meridian's legal counsel, outside firm Hatcher & Boone LLP, reviewed OCC Interpretive Letter 1170 (July 22, 2020), which had concluded that national banks may provide cryptocurrency custody services as a modern form of traditional safekeeping. Based on this interpretive letter, Hatcher & Boone advised Meridian that cryptocurrency custody was a permissible banking activity and that the bank could begin offering services immediately, provided it maintained adequate internal controls. Meridian began onboarding its first three institutional clients on November 1, 2021.

On November 18, 2021, the OCC issued Interpretive Letter 1179. Meridian's compliance team flagged the new letter and initiated an internal review. By this point, Meridian had already executed custody agreements with two hedge funds and one family office, holding approximately $85 million in digital assets. Meridian had not communicated with its OCC supervisory office about the planned cryptocurrency custody services prior to launching them, though its internal controls were robust and well-documented.

Meridian's general counsel argued that since OCC Interpretive Letter 1170 had already established the legal permissibility of cryptocurrency custody, the bank had no obligation to seek any further approval or notification before commencing the activity. The compliance department disagreed, citing the new November 2021 guidance. The bank's audit committee has convened an emergency meeting to determine whether Meridian is in compliance with current OCC requirements and what remedial steps, if any, are necessary.

The OCC's resident examiner, upon learning of Meridian's crypto custody operations during a routine quarterly meeting on December 3, 2021, raised concerns about the bank's failure to follow proper procedures. Meridian's management contends that the bank's strong risk management infrastructure should satisfy any supervisory requirements, and that the November 2021 letter merely restated existing law without imposing new conditions.
question: Under OCC Interpretive Letter 1179, what specific procedural step must a national bank complete before engaging in cryptocurrency custody services addressed in Interpretive Letters 1170, 1172, and 1174, and what specific determination must the OCC supervisory office make before the bank may proceed? Given that Meridian launched its crypto custody services on November 1, 2021 — before IL 1179 was issued on November 18, 2021 — but after IL 1170 had confirmed legal permissibility, is Meridian in compliance, and what is the precise procedural deficiency identified by IL 1179 that IL 1170 alone did not require?
correct_answer:
OCC Interpretive Letter 1179, issued November 18, 2021, clarifies that while the activities addressed in Interpretive Letters 1170, 1172, and 1174 remain legally permissible, a bank must notify its supervisory office in writing of its intention to engage in any of these cryptocurrency activities. Critically, IL 1179 establishes that the bank 'should not engage in the activities until it receives written notification of the supervisory office's non-objection.' This is a specific two-step procedural requirement: (1) written notification to the supervisory office, and (2) receipt of written supervisory non-objection before commencing the activity.

In deciding whether to grant supervisory non-objection, the supervisory office will evaluate the adequacy of the bank's risk management systems and controls, and risk measurement systems, to determine whether the bank can engage in the proposed activities in a safe and sound manner. IL 1179 grounds this requirement in the principle that 'a proposed activity cannot be part of the business of banking if the bank lacks the capacity to conduct the activity in a safe and sound manner.' Thus, mere legal permissibility under IL 1170 is necessary but not sufficient — the bank must also demonstrate operational capacity through the non-objection process.

Meridian is not in compliance as of November 18, 2021, because IL 1179 imposed a supervisory non-objection requirement that did not exist under IL 1170 standing alone. IL 1170 concluded that crypto custody was a permissible form of traditional safekeeping but did not require prior written notification to or written non-objection from the supervisory office. Meridian's reliance solely on IL 1170 was arguably reasonable before November 18, 2021, but after that date, the bank is operating without the required written supervisory non-objection. The fact that Meridian has robust internal controls is relevant to the substantive evaluation the supervisory office would conduct, but it does not substitute for the procedural requirement of obtaining written non-objection before engaging in the activity. Meridian must immediately notify its supervisory office in writing and cease or suspend crypto custody activities until it receives written non-objection.
why_adversarial: This question requires knowing the specific procedural mechanism introduced by IL 1179 — the written notification plus written supervisory non-objection requirement — which was NOT part of IL 1170. A general LLM would know that IL 1170 permitted crypto custody and might assume that permissibility equals authorization to proceed. The precise threshold here is the two-step written process (notify in writing, then receive written non-objection) and the specific safe-and-sound capacity standard that IL 1179 layered onto the earlier interpretive letters. Without reading IL 1179's actual text, a model would likely conflate 'legally permissible' with 'authorized to engage in' and miss the supervisory gate-keeping function entirely.
common_wrong_answer: A general LLM would likely conclude that since OCC Interpretive Letter 1170 already established that cryptocurrency custody is a permissible banking activity, and since Meridian has robust risk management controls, the bank is in compliance. The model would likely say that IL 1179 merely 'reiterated' existing guidance and that Meridian's strong internal controls satisfy any supervisory expectations. It might reference general OCC safety and soundness standards without identifying the specific written notification and written non-objection procedural requirements that IL 1179 uniquely imposed as prerequisites before a bank may commence crypto activities.
applicable_standard: OCC Interpretive Letter 1179 (November 18, 2021); OCC Interpretive Letter 1170 (July 22, 2020); OCC Interpretive Letter 1172 (September 21, 2020); OCC Interpretive Letter 1174 (January 4, 2021); 12 CFR Part 9 (OCC Fiduciary Activities Regulation); OCC safe and sound banking principles

fact_pattern:
Midwestern Heritage Savings Association ('MHSA'), a federally chartered thrift institution headquartered in Columbus, Ohio, has operated a trust department since 1987 under its fiduciary powers granted by the Office of Thrift Supervision. In March 2001, MHSA served as trustee for the Carolyn Drexler Irrevocable Trust, a $4.2 million trust established in 1994 for the benefit of Carolyn's three adult children. The trust instrument was silent on the applicable investment standard, containing only a general grant of investment discretion to the trustee.

MHSA's trust investment committee, led by Senior Vice President Alan Kirchner, allocated 72% of the trust portfolio to a concentrated position in utility stocks and municipal bonds, reasoning that these conservative holdings were consistent with what a prudent person would do with their own property. The committee did not conduct a formal analysis of overall portfolio risk-return optimization, did not consider the beneficiaries' individual financial circumstances or other assets, and did not document any consideration of diversification across asset classes. Instead, Kirchner relied on his 30 years of personal experience managing similar conservative portfolios and his view that utilities and municipals represented 'safe' investments that any reasonable person would select for their own holdings.

In June 2001, following a sharp decline in utility stocks after the Enron revelations began, the trust lost approximately $1.1 million in value. Beneficiary David Drexler filed a complaint with the OTS alleging that MHSA breached its fiduciary duty by failing to diversify the portfolio and by failing to apply modern portfolio theory principles. MHSA defended its actions by arguing that its investment approach satisfied the applicable prudence standard because each individual investment was one that a person of ordinary prudence would make with their own property.

During the OTS examination, examiners reviewed MHSA's fiduciary activities under OTS Trust and Asset Management Handbook Section 110, which was current as of July 2001.
